editorials.title: Presumed ineligible: On the Election Commission of India’s SIR process
editorials.passage:
Not one eligible elector should be left out of the electoral rolls. This statement appears in nearly every document released by the Election Commission of India (ECI) as part of the ongoing SIR process , and the Supreme Court of India, which is hearing petitions challenging the SIR, has also used this refrain. Yet, according to an ECI counter-affidavit filed in the Court, by early September 2026, out of more than 38 lakh appeals submitted to SIR appellate tribunals in West Bengal, just over 1,22,000 appeals were disposed of (a disposal rate of just 3.2%) and 1,13,943 electors were added back to the rolls (an inclusion rate of nearly 93%). This suggests that the claims/corrections phase in the West Bengal SIR — during which judicial officers deployed for verification deemed 27 lakh of the 60 lakh electors flagged for “logical discrepancies” to be ineligible — was deeply flawed. More than 22 lakh of those found ineligible have since appealed, and ECI data show that more than nine in 10 cases decided by the tribunals have ended with the electors back on the rolls. If these “inclusion” and “disposal” rates hold, the majority of the 27 lakh electors should not have been ineligible in the first place and are now struggling to get back on the rolls — an indication that massive disenfranchisement preceded the West Bengal Assembly polls. With municipal elections in the State approaching, the ECI must speed up the appellate process and restore eligible electors to the rolls.

In Phase 3 of the SIR, The Hindu ’s analysis found that in 24 out of Delhi’s 70 constituencies, the draft roll now records fewer electors than those who voted in the February 2025 Assembly election. Such large-scale deletion cannot hold unless there was a major migration process in the capital region or large numbers of voters were never ordinarily resident in Delhi. A more plausible answer is that the enumeration itself has struck off actual voters. The process puts the onus of proving eligibility on the elector, and the ECI’s dropping of enumeration forms at homes has not translated into full enumeration. Requiring electors to link themselves to rolls drawn in the early 2000s then manufactures “discrepancies” even when documents are valid. In Delhi, this “mapping” has put 13.79 lakh electors under notice with a further 19.33 lakh flagged for “logical discrepancies” on undefined grounds. While hearing the Bihar SIR petitions, the Court had intervened sharply to stop eligible voters from being struck off. Its permissiveness in the year since, towards an insouciant ECI has allowed disenfranchisement on a scale that will remain a black mark on the jurisprudence of universal adult franchise in India. As the Court hears petitions on Delhi and West Bengal, it must compel the ECI to reverse course.

editorials.title: Unsafe space: On the U.S. and ‘on-orbit space control weapons‘
editorials.passage:
Although the U.S. military doctrine was openly considering offensive and defensive space control by 2025, the admission on September 14 by U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink, and confirmed by Space Force chief Gen. Douglas Schiess, that the country has deployed “on-orbit space control weapons” to “defend against hostile adversary action” is cause for concern. Satellite systems increasingly underpin communications, energy, and financial networks and many commercial systems serve civilian and military users. To that end, the U.S., Russia, China, and India, among others, have been developing counter-space capabilities while contributing to the technological and strategic environment rendering earth orbit the next major battlefield. The increasing military use of commercial satellites can endanger the protections they enjoy under international humanitarian law even as this law is underprepared for satellites being highly interconnected and often dual-use. That said, the details that justify the need for orbital defence systems also make poorly specified weapons a potential cause of instability. Mr. Meink described the weapon as defensive, but U.S. military doctrine defines “space control” as encompassing both offensive and defensive operations.

Compounding the consequences of confusion when two steerable satellites approach each other without understanding the other’s intentions — including due to future autonomous satellites running artificial intelligence models onboard — is the lack of policy details. What constitutes “hostile action” and what the weapon can do remain unclear. While the Outer Space Treaty does not ban weapons in orbit per se, Article IV prohibits nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit — a fluid line considering the centrality of satellite-based networks for contemporary society and the ability of conventional weapons to render damage en masse; its Article III also requires space activities to comply with international law. But when an autonomous, dual-use orbital asset operated by a commercial entity initiates an unwanted defensive strike, the existing rules, including the Liability Convention, cannot be applied straightforwardly to determine accountability. The rules have become too coarse for what contemporary technologies, and the declining esteem for a rules-based world order, warrant. The U.N. Open-Ended Working Group on the ‘Prevention of an Arms Race in Outer Space’ should offer governments an opportunity to address the disclosure. The U.S. government should also reveal the particulars of the weapons it has deployed, and enter into a multilateral governance arrangement that defines exact thresholds of action and escalation.

editorials.title: Put plastic challenge at the top of India's sustainability battle
editorials.passage: Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s assertion that India’s development is ‘speedy as well as sustainable’ is aligned with the country’s outlook based on its nationally determined contributions (NDC) for 2031-35. It explains why he pointed out the inequality meted out to developing countries at the climate negotiations table. The PM flagged the historical narrative that developed countries get away with six times higher emissions, but developing nations take the blame for their carbon footprints. Listing out achievements in renewable energy, electric mobility, water conservation and natural farming, Modi said the country, having achieved its Paris Agreement commitments made in 2015, enjoys a unique position within the G20 on non-fossil fuels and solar capacity benchmarks.When the government approved the NDC for submission to the UN Framework Convention for Climate Change in March, it carefully designed its targets amid the West Asia crisis. India has achieved its goals on emission intensity and energy transition. But if it truly wants to demonstrate that rapid growth can coexist with environmental responsibility, it must take plastic pollution seriously. Government data put India’s plastic waste generation at 1.76 million tonne in 2024-25, down from 4.1 million tonne in 2022-23. However, the estimate is conservative given it mostly counted urban areas. A Central Pollution Control Board assessment in 2018 had measured plastic waste generation at 25,940 tonne a day, almost 9.5 million tonne annually. That’s the kind of level a study published in Nature echoed in 2024 when it placed India as the top plastic polluter far ahead of China, holding it accountable for nearly a fifth of global plastic emissions..The enormity of the challenge before India is that plastic has entered every aspect of life and its cost is huge. Some progress has been reported. Under the extended producer responsibility, the government claims 19.6 million tonnes of plastic waste was recycled through registered processors by March 2026. But it is a cumulative figure and recycling alone cannot solve the Himalayan problem at hand.The Prime Minister is right that development and sustainability can go hand in hand. But plastic will be a real test of that proposition. A sustainable India cannot merely recycle. It must produce far less, design packaging for reuse and recovery, improve waste collection and make producers accountable for the entire lifecycle of what they sell. editorials.title: Indian starts well despite bumpy logistics at Asiad
editorials.passage: When it was announced that Japan would host the 2026 Asian Games, athletes and fans assumed the organisers would not have the planning weaknesses often associated with massive multi-discipline sporting events. But even Japan, a country experienced in hosting such events and noted for its efficiency and clockwork-like precision, fumbled on the challenges of executing such an event in the modern era. Athletes felt so short-changed over the last week that the Indian sports ministry had to come up with steps such as involving the diaspora to ensure the country’s athletes do not suffer logistical hardships in their bid to win continental glory.As soon as the organising committee decided they would do away with a traditional Games Village, they did run the risk of facing operational challenges—and sure enough, they came up. For example, the Indian shooting contingent has to travel four hours every day to and from the playing arena, which is far from ideal for preparations. Although some of these drawbacks are understandable in the initial days of a big event, most of them could have been avoided. The distance between spread-out venues, though a troublesome issue, seems to be the new normal. Given the ballooning expenses and increasing global resistance to hosting mega events using public money, international sports meets could be planned in a similar manner in the future. Last week offered some priceless lessons for India, which is hosting the Commonwealth Games 2030 and is bidding to host two more—Olympics 2036 and Asian Games 2038..The Games are about peak performances, too. All the 500-odd Indians in the fray at Nagoya are there to etch their names on the wall of fame. Despite long travel hours, the shooters set the tone with five medals in the first two days. Shooting, a sport that has brought India multiple medals at the Olympics, is expected to boost India’s tally further in Japan. Suchika Tariyal claimed a bronze in the newest sport in the tournament: mixed martial arts. Quimcy Dsouza lost her bronze playoffs by a whisker in another fast-growing sport that made a debut: teqball. With the initial days of hiccups taken in stride, India is getting increasingly serious in the medal hunt. editorials.title: Quick Take | Colouring the subconscious
editorials.passage: A rejected community certificate for a government officer in Tamil Nadu dug up deep prejudices in Indian society. It came to light when Justice D Bharatha Chakravarthy of the Madras High Court set aside a district vigilance committee’s refusal to a customs department employee who claimed he had converted to Hinduism after being born a Christian. What made the case stand out is that the certificate was rejected, the judge noted, because the man is “very fair in colour”, has curly hair, is tall and well-built, and speaks both Tamil and English fluently. As we preach the need to curb casteism, we need to delve deep within our minds to first recognise and then root out prejudices..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Promoted Without Learning
editorials.passage:
In the forest-fringed Toto settlements of Alipurduar and the scattered Birhor hamlets of Purulia, the report cards often tell a reassuring story. Children move from one class to the next every year, enrolment remains steady, and schools appear to be fulfilling the constitutional promise of universal education. But inside the classrooms, a harsher reality unfolds. Many students in Classes VI and VII struggle to read a Class II-level passage or solve elementary arithmetic, exposing a silent learning crisis that experts say was deepened by the implementation of the Right to Education (RTE) Act's now-diluted nodetention policy. 

What was conceived as a progressive reform to eliminate the fear of failure has, in some of India's most disadvantaged communities, evolved into what education researchers describe as "promotion without proficiency"— a system that has succeeded in keeping children in school but often failed to ensure that they actually learn. The no-detention provision, introduced under the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act in 2010, prohibited schools from failing students until the completion of elementary education. The objective was to reduce dropouts, curb examination anxiety and make schools more child-friendly. While the policy improved retention on paper, its implementation gradually exposed a widening disconnect between enrolment and learning outcomes. 

The Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) 2022 offered a sobering snapshot of this crisis. Nationally, only 42.8 per cent of Class V students could read a Class II-level text, while just 25.6 per cent could correctly solve a simple division problem. Educationists believe the situation is considerably more severe in geographically isolated tribal regions, where schools contend with teacher shortages, multigrade classrooms, language barriers and chronic absenteeism. Among West Bengal's Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs), these structural disadvantages have accumulated over years. For the Toto community in Totopara and the Birhor settlements spread across Purulia's forested landscape, education begins with multiple handicaps. 

Many children enter schools where the language of instruction differs from the language spoken at home. One teacher is often responsible for teaching several classes simultaneously. Seasonal migration, forest-based livelihoods and poor transport infrastructure interrupt schooling for weeks at a stretch. Under the earlier no-detention regime, however, these interruptions rarely translated into academic intervention. Students continued to advance with their age cohort regardless of whether they had acquired foundational literacy or numeracy. 

According to anthropologist Dr Santanu Panda, faculty member of the Department of Anthropology at Sukumar Sengupta Mahavidyalaya, Keshpur, the crisis cannot be understood merely as an educational failure but as the outcome of a policy that overlooked the socio-cultural realities of tribal communities. "The no-detention policy emerged from a child-rights perspective and undoubtedly reduced the fear of examinations. But among Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups, the policy was implemented without strengthening the educational ecosystem that children required. Promotion became administrative, not academic," Dr Panda observed. 

He argues that children from communities like the Totos and Birhors often enter school with linguistic and cultural backgrounds very different from mainstream classrooms. Unless early education is delivered in the child's mother tongue and supported by contextual teaching methods, learning deficits begin in the very first years and continue to widen as children move through successive grades. "These children are not academically weak," he said. "The system simply failed to provide the foundational support necessary for meaningful learning." 

Field studies among Birhor communities underline the scale of the challenge. Literacy levels remain significantly below the state average. In villages such as Bhupatipally, literacy stands at around 60.84 per cent, while Bareriya records only 37.68 per cent. Studies estimate that illiteracy among Birhor populations exceeds 60 per cent in several settlements. The Toto community has achieved relatively better educational outcomes but continues to lag behind state averages on several indicators. Teachers working in these areas frequently encounter students in upper primary classes who cannot independently read simple Bengali texts or perform basic mathematical operations. 

As academic content becomes progressively more complex, these children find themselves increasingly alienated from classroom teaching. "Once foundational literacy is lost, every subsequent class becomes more difficult to comprehend," Dr Panda explained. "Eventually, many children remain physically present in school but psychologically disconnected from the learning process." The growing evidence of learning deficits eventually triggered a national policy rethink. In 2019, Parliament amended the RTE Act, allowing states to conduct regular assessments in Classes V and VIII and retain students who fail to achieve minimum learning benchmarks after receiving remedial instruction. 

West Bengal is among the states that have adopted the revised framework. Yet legal scholars caution against interpreting the amendment simply as a return to examination-based education. Dr Vijay Kumar Sinha, Assistant Professor and Vice-Principal (Academics) at the Indian Institute of Legal Studies, Siliguri, said the amendment represents a shift from unconditional promotion towards accountability, but only if implemented alongside educational safeguards. "The original objective of the Right to Education Act was to guarantee access and prevent exclusion. The amendment does not abandon that philosophy; rather, it attempts to reconcile children's rights with learning outcomes," Dr Sinha said. According to him, detention should never become punitive. 

"The amended framework permits retention only after schools have provided remedial instruction and an opportunity for reassessment. The legal intent is to ensure that a child acquires minimum competencies before progressing, not to punish academic weakness." Dr Sinha believes the amendment offers states an opportunity to identify learning gaps early rather than allowing deficiencies to accumulate until secondary education. However, he warned that merely retaining students without improving educational infrastructure would produce limited results. 

"If schools continue to function with inadequate teacher strength, poor connectivity, language mismatches and insufficient academic support, detention alone cannot improve educational outcomes. Policy reform must be accompanied by institutional investment." That institutional deficit remains stark across many tribal habitations of West Bengal. Multi-grade teaching continues to be common. Teachers posted in remote schools often handle several classes simultaneously. During the monsoon, roads leading to schools become virtually inaccessible. Many students miss classes because they accompany their families for seasonal work linked to forests or agriculture. Economic pressures further compound educational exclusion. 

Children who successfully complete elementary education frequently discontinue their studies during secondary school to contribute to household incomes. Researchers studying tribal education have also noted that while parents generally welcomed the nodetention policy because it reduced examination stress, teachers increasingly expressed concern that automatic promotion weakened learning and indirectly contributed to higher dropout rates in later years, particularly among girls. Education experts therefore argue that the debate should move beyond detention versus no-detention. 

The larger challenge lies in ensuring that children master foundational skills before progressing to higher grades. That requires sustained recruitment of teachers in remote schools, early instruction in tribal mother tongues, community participation, flexible academic calendars that account for seasonal migration, targeted remedial programmes and better residential schooling facilities in geographically isolated regions. For Dr Panda, education policy must recognise that equality does not mean treating every child identically. "Children from PVTG communities require culturally responsive education. Uniform policies rarely produce equitable outcomes when starting conditions are fundamentally unequal," he said. 

Dr Sinha echoes that view from a legal perspective. "The constitutional promise of education is not fulfilled simply because a child is enrolled or promoted. The promise is fulfilled only when the child acquires the capability to participate meaningfully in education and society." As West Bengal recalibrates its school education policy following the RTE amendment, the experiences of the Toto and Birhor communities serve as a reminder that enrolment statistics alone cannot measure educational success. 

The no-detention policy may have protected children from the fear of failure, but in many of the state's most vulnerable tribal classrooms, it also concealed years of invisible learning loss. The challenge before policymakers now is not merely to decide when a child should be promoted, but to ensure that every promotion reflects genuine learning rather than administrative progression. For the children growing up in the forests of Totopara and Purulia, that distinction could determine whether education becomes a pathway out of deprivation—or simply another promise left unfulfilled. 


(THE WRITER IS A SENIOR STAFF REPORTER WITH THE STATESMAN)

editorials.title: A time for investing in peace
editorials.passage:
Two September 11s offer two very different lessons for the world. On 11 September 1906, more than 3,000 Indians gathered at Johannesburg’s Empire Theatre and took a solemn pledge to oppose the Transvaal government’s discriminatory registration law without violence. Led by Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, they chose Satyagraha, the force of truth, discipline and non-violent resistance, rather than anger or armed revolt. 

On 11 September 2001, the terrorist attacks in the United States caused immense loss of life and introduced a new era of fear, war and global securitization. Together, these two dates remind us that societies can respond to injustice and insecurity either through violence and suspicion or through truth, restraint and organised civic action. This contrast gains special meaning as the world observes the “International Day of Peace” on 21 September 2026. The United Nations theme for this year is “Invest in Peace – For Everyone, Everywhere, Every Day.” 

The theme calls on governments, institutions, communities and individuals to treat peace as a continuous responsibility rather than as a matter reserved for diplomats and international conferences. Peace-building goes beyond formal negotiations and conference rooms. It requires sustained investment in education, justice, trust, dialogue and social cooperation, along with small but meaningful actions in homes, schools, workplaces and neighbourhoods. The United Nations has described this approach as support for the “everyday architects of peace” – people who help bridge divisions and build safer communities. A reference to the 1906 gathering in Johannesburg is poignant. 

For it was an early example of such organised civic action. The law required Indians to register, provide fingerprints and carry passes. Instead of obeying an unjust order or responding with violence, the community chose to stand together, speak openly and accept the possible consequences of resistance under Gandhi who first experimented with his principle of non-violence on foreign soil against the might of the time through this powerful declaration of “Satyagraha”. 

This was the beginning of Satyagraha as a collective method. It showed that ordinary people could challenge injustice through courage, self-discipline and non-cooperation. Satyagraha is often translated as “truth-force” or “soul-force.” The word combines satya, meaning truth, and agraha, meaning firm insistence or holding firmly. It was not passive behaviour. It required people to identify injustice, organise peacefully, refuse cooperation with wrong, and accept suffering without seeking revenge. Its purpose was not to destroy the opponent but to appeal to conscience and expose the injustice of the system. Ninety-five years later, the events of September 11 produced a very different response. 

Unlike the mass movement inspired by Gandhi’s call for non-violence and peaceful resistance in 1906, the terrorist attacks on the United States triggered a global shift towards military intervention, heightened security and counterterrorism measures. Governments across the world expanded military operations, strengthened surveillance systems, enhanced intelligence networks and established or empowered security institutions to prevent future attacks. Airports, public spaces and international borders came under stricter security controls, while new laws were introduced to monitor financial transactions, track suspected terrorist networks and improve intelligence sharing between nations. 

Although these measures were intended to protect citizens and address emerging security threats, they also raised important questions about privacy, civil liberties, human rights and the balance between national security and individual freedom. The post-9/11 world thus demonstrated how fear and violence could reshape international relations, influencing government policies and public life for decades while highlighting the continuing challenge of addressing conflict through dialogue, cooperation and peaceful means. While such measures may be necessary to prevent immediate threats, force and surveillance alone cannot create lasting peace. 

They cannot, by themselves, build trust, address discrimination, heal social divisions or remove the conditions that allow violence to grow. This is why the idea of peace as an investment is important. Investment means putting resources, time and attention into the conditions that allow people to live with dignity and resolve differences without violence. It includes good education, accessible healthcare, fair policing, legal aid, employment opportunities, accountable institutions and spaces where people from different communities can meet and listen to one another. 

A practical peace agenda, therefore, should focus on four important areas. First, schools, universities, police academies and public institutions should teach negotiation, mediation, media literacy, restorative justice and non-violent communication to help people resolve conflicts peacefully. Second, communities should encourage neighbourhood mediation centres, interfaith discussions, cultural exchange programmes and local peace committees to build trust and understanding. Third, peace requires justice and dignity through fair treatment, protection of human rights, access to legal support and transparent action against discrimination. 

Finally, media organizations and public campaigns should promote cooperation, reconciliation, empathy and the efforts of local peace builders rather than focusing only on conflict, fear and division. These goals can be measured. Institutions can record the number of people trained in mediation, the reduction in school suspensions and use-of-force incidents, the number of disputes settled through dialogue, and public perceptions of fairness and safety. They can also examine whether different social groups feel equally heard and protected. Everyday Satyagraha does not require a grand march or a historic gathering. It can begin with listening before judging, refusing to spread unverified information, intervening safely when someone is being targeted, apologising when harm has been caused and working with people from another community on a shared public project. 

Schools can teach children how to resolve disagreements. Neighbourhoods can create mediation networks. Local media can report not only on violence but also on the people who prevent it. The idea of “peace investment” encourages us to look at public money in a different way. Money spent on training teachers, mediators, police officers and community leaders should not be seen simply as government expenditure. It is an investment in preventing violence and resolving problems before they become serious conflicts. Similarly, providing legal aid, building fair and accessible institutions, and creating spaces where communities can openly discuss their differences are essential for creating trust between citizens and public institutions. 

When people feel heard, treated fairly and given peaceful ways to resolve disagreements, the chances of conflict and violence can be reduced. Therefore, the success of peace efforts should not be measured only by the number of threats stopped or incidents prevented, but also by how many disputes were resolved peacefully, how much trust was rebuilt, and how many people – especially young people – were given the knowledge and skills to become peace-builders in their families, communities and society. The forthcoming International Day of Non-Violence on 2 October 2026, observed on the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi, reminds the world that peace is not simply the absence of violence. 

It is a way of living based on dialogue, compassion, moral courage, mutual respect and human dignity. Gandhi’s message shows that peaceful action, when guided by truth and courage, can become a powerful force for social change. Thus, all these dates form a meaningful sequence. The first September 11 recalls the birth of organized Satyagraha. The second reminds us of the devastating consequences of violence and fear. 

The International Day of Peace asks us to invest in the conditions that make peace possible, while the International Day of Non-Violence invites us to practice those values in everyday life. Peace, in this sense, is not a seasonal slogan or the absence of war. It is a permanent civic commitment, for everyone, everywhere, every day. 

The writer is Programme Executive,Gandhi Samriti and Darshan Samriti

editorials.title: Ecological failures
editorials.passage:
That Comptroller and Auditor General’s performance audit of the Green India Mission is very troubling. India does not lack ambition on paper. There are schemes, targets, budgets and repeated commitments to use forests as a bulwark against climate change. What is in short supply, the CAG audit suggests, is delivery. Between 2015-16 and 2024-25, the Mission aimed to increase forest and tree cover over 1.4 million hectares. 

The actual increase was only about 30,000 hectares ~ a shortfall of approximately 97.57 per cent. The record on improving degraded forests is scarcely better. Against a target of 1.4 million hectares, improvement was achieved over only around 110,000 hectares. The CAG points to inadequate planning, weak financial management, insufficient monitoring and poor coordination among government agencies. But the audit also exposes a deeper problem: the tendency to confuse planting trees with creating forests. A forest cannot be produced by treating afforestation as an administrative exercise in planting a prescribed number of saplings. It takes time and ecological knowledge. 

It requires suitable land, appropriate species, long-term maintenance, careful management of soil and water, participation by local communities and sustained monitoring. The crucial question is not how many saplings were planted, but what became of them. How many survived? What is their condition after five years? Have they become part of a functioning ecosystem? Has vegetation reduced soil erosion and improved water retention? Has biodiversity recovered? Without such measures, impressive plantation figures can conceal ecological failure. This is also why the language of “green cover” can mislead. 

A landscape filled with trees is not necessarily a forest. Rows of commercially planted trees may increase vegetation without recreating the ecological complexity of an existing forest. A forest is a living system ~ of trees, soil, fungi, insects, birds, animals, water and innumerable relationships that evolve over decades, often centuries. The choice of species is therefore critical. The CAG audit drew attention to plantations involving Acacia auriculiformis, a species identified in the audit as invasive. If afforestation introduces species that damage local ecosystems or suppress native vegetation, the objective of ecological restoration is defeated. 

We should remember that planting trees and restoring forests are not the same thing. Monoculture plantations may be easier to administer and count. They may also produce attractive numbers in official reports. Ecological restoration is harder. It requires an understanding of local landscapes and a commitment extending far beyond the plantation season. It cannot be reduced to an annual drive followed by a ceremonial photograph. The timing of financial allocations is another revealing problem. Afforestation is seasonal. Saplings must be planted at the right time, particularly in relation to rainfall. When funds reach implementing agencies after the planting season has passed, saplings are often put into the ground under unfavourable conditions, with predictable consequences for their survival. 

The monsoon will not wait for a file to move from one department to another. There is an even larger contradiction at the heart of India’s approach to forests. The Green India Mission cannot by itself protect forests while existing natural ecosystems continue to face pressure from infrastructure expansion, mining and urban development. The crucial questions extend beyond plantation targets. How is a forest defined? Which land is recognised as forest? How much forest land is diverted for development projects? How seriously are the views of local and indigenous communities considered? 

The proposed cutting of thousands of trees in Delhi’s Shahabad Mohammadpur “deemed forest” for railway infrastructure, which prompted judicial intervention, illustrated one such conflict. The Hasdeo Arand region in central India ~ one of the country’s important contiguous forest landscapes ~ offers another reminder that formal protection does not necessarily guarantee ecological security. On the one hand, public money is spent on ambitious programmes to plant millions of new trees. On the other, mature forests ~ ecosystems shaped over decades ~ are cleared or fragmented for development. 

The two processes are not equivalent. A sapling planted today cannot compensate for the destruction of an old forest. Nor can a plantation quickly reproduce the biodiversity, carbon storage, soil systems and hydrological functions of a mature ecosystem. Destroying a forest is relatively easy. Growing one is not. This raises an uncomfortable question: are afforestation targets sometimes being used as a form of moral accounting? Trees are destroyed in one place, saplings planted elsewhere, and the environmental balance sheet is considered settled. Nature does not work that way. 

In an age of climate change, forests are not simply scenic landscapes or carbon sinks. They are critical ecological infrastructure. They hold soil together, protect watersheds, improve water retention and reduce the impact of floods and erosion. Forested landscapes support an extraordinary range of biodiversity and play a crucial role in sustaining freshwater systems. Afforestation, therefore, cannot remain an isolated project of an environment department. 

It must be linked to agriculture, water management, rural livelihoods, disaster preparedness and public health. Approaches such as agroforestry and homestead-based tree cultivation deserve greater attention because they can integrate tree cover with livelihoods and land use. But here too, ecological suitability must remain central. More trees do not automatically produce healthier ecosystems. What India needs is a fundamental change in its approach to afforestation. Forests should not be treated as targets to be ticked off in annual reports but as living ecological and social assets. They are not simply “green cover”. 

They contain soil, water, plants, animals and complex forms of interdependence. In many parts of India, they are also inseparable from the livelihoods, cultures and knowledge systems of local and indigenous communities. Afforestation programmes should be judged by long-term survival, ecological restoration, biodiversity recovery, soil health and water retention. Independent monitoring must continue well beyond the plantation phase. Local communities should be partners in planning and protecting forests, not merely providers of labour. 

Above all, protecting existing natural forests must take precedence over the symbolic expansion of plantation targets. As mountains are blasted, forests fragmented and rivers placed under increasing pressure, disasters are often described as nature’s revenge. But nature does not take revenge. When human greed and short-sighted development weaken forests, wetlands, mountains and river systems, these ecosystems gradually lose their capacity to absorb shocks. 

Floods become more destructive, slopes more unstable and droughts more severe. Planting a sapling matters. But planting a sapling is not the same as growing a forest. Until policy recognises that distinction, India may continue to celebrate plantation targets while quietly losing the ecosystems those targets were meant to protect. 

(The writer is Professor, Department of English and Culture Studies and Director, Centre for Australian Studies, the University of Burdwan)

editorials.title: Pakistan is playing games with FATF
editorials.passage:
Pakistan recently announced a reward of Rs 70 lakh for information leading to the arrest of Jaish-e-Mohammed (JEM) chief, Masood Azhar, who is a UNSC-designated terrorist. The timing appears to indicate that it is aimed at avoiding being questioned by the FATF (Financial Action Task Force) in its forthcoming plenary. Pakistan was last placed on the FATF grey list in 2018 and removed in 2022, after meeting some conditions. It has been repeatedly cautioned that exiting the grey list does not provide immunity from monitoring and it will remain under regular evaluation by the Asia Pacific group. 

The next detailed audit is due in 2029. Remaining on the grey list implies that the country has flaws in its money laundering and counter-terrorist financing systems. A country on the grey list loses on foreign investment (reportedly around 7 per cent) and pays higher borrowing costs while multilateral development banks and donor nations are compelled to reassess funding arrangements. It also impacts the country’s global reputation and standing. Pakistan has itself admitted that it lost about USD 38 billion in economic growth and GDP after being placed on the grey list multiple times since 2008. 

It fears this will be repeated if it is again targeted. A US Congress report of March this year mentions that 12 out of 15 terrorist groups operating from Pakistan are marked as Foreign Terrorist Organizations by them. Many of them are aimed at India. Since 2018 Pakistan has been designated by the US as a ‘country of particular concern.’ A 2018 UNSC updated list of terrorists, under the UN 1267 Al Qaeda Sanctions Committee, included 139 based in Pakistan. Current inputs mention that these are now around a hundred. The number of terrorists sought by India from Pakistan has been increasing. The number has risen from 1330 in 2021 to 1804 currently, an increase of 35 per cent. 

Wanted in India for various terrorist incidents, they roam freely in Pakistan, protected by their security agencies. This indicates the growing terror infrastructure within Pakistan. Evidently, the country plays host to many of the world’s most dangerous terrorists, whose existence it continues to deny. The FATF is scheduled to hold its plenary meeting from 26 to 30 October in Paris. Pakistan is desperate to show the global financial body that it is serious in its commitment to counter terrorism. It therefore increased the bounty on Masood Azhar from Rupees 50 to 70 lakh. 

It hopes this would convince the global body of its intent. It is aware that India is watching every move. Azhar, the founder and chief of the JEM, is wanted in India for multiple crimes, including the 2001 Parliament attack and the 2008 Mumbai attack. His group has also been linked to the 2016 Pathankot base attack and the 2019 Pulwama bombing. Pakistan listed Azhar as a wanted terrorist in its Federal Investigation Agency’s Red Book in 2021 and repeated this in 2026. FIRs have been registered against him in Pakistan in 2020 and 2021, and he has even been declared missing. 

Pakistan had claimed that Azhar had left the country for Afghanistan, which Kabul denied. It is known that Azhar is hidden and protected by the Pakistan army, moved from place to place to prevent being targeted by unknown gunmen. It is reported that Azhar is more secure than Pakistan’s political leadership. India responded to Pakistan’s actions with the MEA spokesperson mentioning, “Such gimmicks and hoodwinking by Pakistan are nothing new. We have seen similar gimmicks in the past as well.” He added, “For a state sponsor of terrorism to make such phoney announcements, we all know how hollow it is. Pakistan must take concrete action and not make phoney announcements.” 

JEM operates from Bahawalpur and its base was destroyed by Indian forces in Operation Sindoor. The strike killed 10 members of Azhar’s family and four of his aides. Reports indicate that the Pakistan government and the ISI released Rs 25 crore to rebuild the base. It is currently operational. The JEM is also attempting to raise Rs 3.91 billion to create 313 new markaz for which more than 290 online payment wallets are being used, a fact which cannot be hidden. Interestingly, the supposedly missing Azhar released a press statement after the Indian strike on Bahawalpur which said, “Ten members of my family including five children, my elder sister and her husband, my Islamic scholar nephew, his wife and my niece, in addition to this my old friend Hazifa, his mother and two other colleagues were killed.” He also announced the timing for the funeral. 

It is unlikely that the Pakistan army would have permitted him to be present. Despite this, Pakistan claims it is unaware of zhar’s whereabouts. Simultaneously, Indian intelligence sources have mentioned that Azhar is currently housed in Nawabshah in Sindh. In September last year, Masood Ilyas Kashmiri, a JEM commander, claimed that orders for military personnel to attend the funeral of terrorists killed in Operation Sindoor were given directly by then army chief, now field marshal, Asim Munir. 

Photographic evidence of senior Pakistan army and police officers as also local politicians being present exists, adding credence to the fact that Pakistan remains a state supporter of terrorism. The irony is that Pakistan is offering money to locate a terrorist who, apart from operating from its soil for decades, is protected by its own security agencies. It is not that the world is unaware of Pakistan’s support to terrorism and that the increase in the reward for Azhar is only a smokescreen. 

Its major advantage for now is support from the US, especially as it attempts to broker talks between Washington and Tehran. The reality is that the state supporting terrorism against all its neighbours - India, Afghanistan and Iran - is today embroiled in its own internal security crisis. Pakistan’s chances of emerging from the growing menace of freedom movements in its western provinces unscathed is almost non-existent. India has to sit back, bring out the popcorn and watch Pakistan burn, all because of its own flawed policies. The FATF must ignore Pakistan’s drama on Azhar and once again push for initiating steps for its re-entry into the grey list. 

The writer is a retired Major-General of the Indian Army

editorials.title: Political Shells
editorials.passage:
India’s democracy has no shortage of political parties. The more troubling question is whether every organisation carrying the legal identity of a political party is actually functioning as one. More than 2,800 Registered Unrecognised Political Parties are on the Election Commission’s rolls. Many are perfectly legitimate small movements, and electoral insignificance cannot itself be treated as evidence of wrongdoing. But the financial numbers reported by some of these parties point to a problem that goes well beyond the normal untidiness of India’s multi-party democracy. 

Consider the scale. One Gujarat-based party reported receiving about Rs 330 crore in donations in 2023-24, although it subsequently fielded only one Lok Sabha candidate. Another party reported donations rising from Rs 216 crore to more than Rs 620 crore in a year, despite also fielding only one candidate. Six such parties together reported roughly Rs 1,700 crore in donations while putting up just 15 candidates in the 2024 general election. The issue is not electoral success. It is whether the political-party framework is being used for purposes that have little to do with politics. That possibility matters because the tax system deliberately gives political donations a privileged status. Eligible contributions to political parties can provide taxpayers with deductions, subject to statutory conditions. 

This creates an incentive on both sides: somebody may want a tax deduction, while somebody else controls an entity capable of receiving the contribution. If intermediaries begin connecting the two, a political party can become something very different from an organisation competing for votes. This is why the reported Income Tax Department scrutiny is significant. An internal document identified Rs 5,591 crore in suspected bogus political donations and Rs 665 crore in foreign transactions requiring scrutiny. Those figures are allegations or investigative leads, not findings of guilt. But they indicate that the potential problem is far larger than the accounts of a few obscure parties. The Election Commission has already recognised part of the institutional weakness. 

It has moved against hundreds of Registered Unrecognised Political Parties that had remained inactive for years. Yet removing an inactive party from the Commission’s list does not necessarily eliminate its legal existence or resolve the financial questions surrounding it. The answer, however, cannot simply be to eliminate small parties. Democratic pluralism requires room for new political movements, including those that initially attract few votes. What needs scrutiny is the privilege attached to registration. 

A political organisation receiving Rs 100 crore, Rs 200 crore or Rs 600 crore should be able to demonstrate who controls it, who finances it, how the money is spent and what political activity it actually conducts. A democracy should make it easy to start a political movement, but difficult to turn a political identity into a financial shell. That is the real warning in these extraordinary numbers. The danger is not that India’s political system has too many parties. It is that some parties may have acquired a financial life vastly larger than their political one.

editorials.title: Arctic Bargain
editorials.passage:
The emerging agreement between the United States and Denmark over Greenland may have eased a dangerous transatlantic confrontation, but it has also exposed a deeper challenge facing the international order: how to reconcile the security ambitions of powerful states with the sovereignty and self-determination of smaller territories. President Donald Trump’s campaign to acquire Greenland, including threats of military action, placed an extraordinary strain on relations within NATO. 

The proposed settlement offers a diplomatic alternative to confrontation, but its significance extends well beyond the immediate dispute. Greenland is becoming a test of whether strategic necessity can be invoked to justify arrangements that substantially alter the rights of those who inhabit a territory. Washington’s interest is not difficult to understand. Greenland occupies a critical position between North America and Europe, overlooking important Arctic and North Atlantic approaches. Its importance is likely to grow as melting ice opens new maritime routes and intensifies competition over resources. The United States also regards the island as integral to its missile-defence ambitions and to containing Russian and Chinese influence in the Arctic. 

Yet geography does not confer ownership. Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark, and its population has a recognised right to determine its political future. Any security arrangement that treats Greenland as strategic real estate risks reducing its people to spectators in decisions affecting their homeland. The reported provisions of the agreement raise questions that cannot be settled by diplomatic declarations alone. Expanded American military access, the ability to construct additional installations and restrictions on investments by countries outside NATO could significantly shape Greenland’s future. 

If these powers are intended to endure even after possible independence, the implications become more consequential. Greenlanders could inherit a state whose security choices have already been constrained. There is also an institutional question for NATO. The alliance rests on collective defence and the principle that its members’ security is interconnected. A dispute in which one member threatens the territory of another exposes the limits of solidarity when national interests collide. A negotiated settlement may restore cooperation, but it cannot erase the precedent created by coercive diplomacy. The absence of a published agreement is therefore more than a procedural inconvenience. Denmark’s parliamentary scrutiny and Greenland’s democratic consent will be essential to establishing whether the arrangement genuinely protects the territory or merely accommodates competing claims over it. 

The existing American defence presence also makes transparency necessary: the public deserves to know what additional powers Washington is seeking and why. Greenland’s mineral wealth adds an economic dimension. Investment can support development, infrastructure and employment, but strategic competition must not deprive Greenlanders of meaningful control over their resources. The Arctic needs cooperation, not a contest in which sovereignty becomes negotiable under pressure. A durable settlement must provide credible security guarantees while preserving Greenland’s democratic agency. Otherwise, this bargain may postpone rather than resolve the fundamental conflict at its heart.

editorials.title: A trailblazer
editorials.passage:
Over the past half a century, ‘Bengali entrepreneurship’ has come to be seen as an oxymoron. Bengali entrepreneurs who survived, like the Nags of IFB and the Chatterjees of Luxmi Tea and Obeetee carpets mainly operated outside Bengal. Even adopted-Bengali groups, like those headed by Harsh Goenka and the late Aditya Birla, have left the state.

This is ironic, since India’s first modern entrepreneur was a remarkable Bengali, Dwarkanath Tagore, the Elon Musk of his era, who was a pioneer of what is today called private equity investing: buying into underperforming businesses, turning them around (often into world-beaters), and then selling the rejuvenated business. Dwarkanath’s portrait continues to adorn the walls at both the Bengal Chamber of Commerce and The Bengal Club, but ought also to inspire new generations of entrepreneurs as Bengal seeks a new industrial dawn.

Between 1831 and 1846, Dwarkanath was the world’s leading entrepreneur, creating some of the greatest firms of his time but also suffering a few spectacular failures (how would you be a true entrepreneur otherwise?). Inheriting a relatively modest zamindari , he grew it rapidly, becoming the second-largest contributor to land revenue in greater Bengal. But he pioneered in using his lands to build up extensive export industries in silk, sugar, rum and indigo which soon made him the biggest exporter in British India.

He also founded the largest newspapers in India, and was the leading patron of the theatre in Calcutta. When several major banks of British India collapsed in 1830-33, Dwarkanath bought them at rock-bottom prices and integrated them into his Union Bank, which became India’s largest bank in short order.

In 1835, he bought a struggling coal mine in Ranigunj and turned it into India’s first truly world class colliery, employing British engineers and technicians alongside several Indian (including Indo-Portuguese) managers and Santhal workers. The British began to import coal from Newcastle to undermine his growing market clout.

So when the Opium War spurred additional demand for coal, Dwarkanath initially held back supplies to teach the British a lesson — until they came begging for him to relent! Although Dwarkanath sold his shares after about a decade, the Bengal Coal Company he created remained India’s largest private coal company for 140 years.

He also created an extensive network of steam tugboats across Bengal and North India, eventually acquiring several shipping lines that formed one of the world’s largest fleets to take his coal and indigo to markets around the world. In a famous race to carry cargo quickest between Calcutta and Canton, Dwarkanath’s clippers comfortably beat those of Rustomji Cowasji Banaji. Those clippers carried opium, the leading commodity of that era (although opium trade was a negligible part of Tagore’s business).

When the Manchu Chinese dynasty’s commissioner, Lin Zexu, seized all the opium stored in Canton (Guangzhou) and arrested Lancelot Dent, the second-largest trader of opium in the city, it became the casus belli for the First Opium War between Britain and China. It was to protest Dent’s arrest that William Jardine (Canton’s biggest opium trader) persuaded the British foreign secretary, (later prime minister) Lord Palmerston, to launch that war. Dwarkanath’s clipper, Ariel , was one of those forced to give up its cargo to Commissioner Lin, but the loss of one clipper’s cargo barely did Tagore much harm.

With one of his subordinates, William Prinsep, Dwarkanath then established India’s first tea estates, creating the Assam Company, which still claims him as part of its illustrious pedigree. He and Prinsep had established the Bengal Tea Association, aiming to have an Indian board, albeit with links to a London financing company. After the merger with the London entity, Dwarkanath’s share in the Assam Company dwindled to 5% although Prinsep joined the London board once he returned to England.

As to the failures, Dwarkanath’s attempt to manufacture sugar in India (on the Caribbean model) failed, but he switched to making gur and rum instead. Prinsep’s attempts at manufacturing salt were a colossal failure as was his expensive proposal to build a bridge of boats across the Hooghly.

Dwarkanath sold his shares in the Union Bank in 1845 but the bank had become too concentrated in a single industry — indigo — which brought about its downfall two years after Tagore had sold his shares. Had Dwarkanath still been involved, he would have tided the bank over the temporary difficulty caused by a decline in its asset values (foreclosed indigo factories), but his successors were incapable of managing matters as only a pioneer could.

That his sons showed scant business acumen was a crucial reason why he sold-off shares in his key businesses. Dwarkanath himself died in 1846 on a stormy night at St George’s (now Brown’s) Hotel, London. One of his English journalistic protégés wrote that the skies themselves had thundered unprecedentedly at the passing of this truly great man.

Dwarkanath had pioneered the managing-agency business model that British Calcutta came to rely on, although Britons carefully ensured that no Indian would ever again become as powerful as him. One that did emerge in the 1890s was Rajendra Nath Mookerjee’s Martin & Co. (later Martin Burn), which built most of the iconic buildings of Calcutta's business district, the Ujjayanta palace in Tripura, Belur Math (the headquarters of the Ramakrishna Mission), and established the ironworks at Kulti.

The swadeshi movement to protest the 1905 partition of Bengal spawned numerous new enterprises: P.C. Ray’s Bengal Chemicals and Pharmaceuticals (with Acqua Ptychotis, Pheneol and numerous other household brands), Surendra Mohan Bose’s Duckback, Khagendra Das’s Calcutta Chemicals (Margo soap), and P.C. Chatterjee’s Luxmi Tea (founded in Tripura).

After his father’s early death in 1936, Biren Mookerjee vastly expanded the Indian Iron and Steel Co. (IISCO) in Burnpur. In 1953, the very first loan ever made by the World Bank to a private enterprise was made to IISCO, which received another World Bank loan three years later. Known for its engineering acumen and focus on quality, IISCO — like most of the great swadeshi enterprises — became a tragic victim of communist agitation in the 1960s and was nationalised in 1972. Over the subsequent five decades, Bengal became an industrial wasteland, as most iconic Bengali-owned companies were nationalised or closed.

Reviving the entrepreneurial spirit in Bengal requires the re-establishment of a conducive, pro-business climate. Undoing more than a half-century of hostility to markets and business will require a mind-set change among the public. There is a palpable hunger for employment generation in a state that has been starved of opportunity for too long. A strong endorsement of the new labour laws, encouraging agri-processing, stimulating health tourism, and leading in new technologies like AI and EV batteries could provide the breadth of opportunity for modern Dwarkanaths to take flight.

Prasenjit K. Basu is an economist and historian

editorials.title: The ball’s on the other foot
editorials.passage:
Gianni Infantino has retreated. After weeks of mounting opposition, FIFA abandoned plans to sell a stake in the commercial rights of the World Cup to private equity investors. The retreat followed an extraordinary rebellion by UEFA, CONCACAF, senior football officials, and governance critics who warned that the proposal threatened to transform football’s greatest public institution into another financial asset.

The reversal marks a rare political defeat for FIFA’s leadership. Yet the real story is not that Infantino backed down. It is why the proposal emerged in the first place and what it reveals about the accelerating financialisation of global sport.

The abandoned proposal exposed something far more consequential than a failed business strategy. It revealed a growing struggle over the future of the world’s most popular sport. It was about redefining ownership, accountability, and power in international football.

For decades, FIFA has presented itself as the custodian of the global game. Its legitimacy has rested on the claim that revenues generated by the World Cup ultimately serve football itself, funding development projects, supporting smaller federations, and expanding the sport across continents.

Private equity would have altered that relationship fundamentally. Investment funds do not enter institutions to preserve tradition or safeguard public trust. They invest to generate returns. Their obligations run to investors rather than supporters, players, or communities. Once those incentives become embedded in the governance of football’s most valuable tournament, commercial priorities inevitably begin to shape institutional decisions.

That is why the proposal provoked such unusually broad resistance. UEFA’s unprecedented criticism, echoed by CONCACAF and reinforced by senior football officials, reflected more than disagreement over governance. The language employed by FIFA’s critics — warning against opaque decision-making and demanding a broader reckoning with leadership — suggested that confidence had been eroding long before the private equity proposal emerged. Carlos Cordeiro’s resignation from his advisory role underscored the seriousness of the crisis. His public rejection of the plan transformed what might have remained an internal governance dispute into a broader debate about football’s future. Infantino ultimately withdrew the proposal, explaining that it had become too divisive to pursue.

But the economic forces that produced the proposal have not disappeared. Football today occupies an extraordinary position within the global entertainment economy. Broadcasting rights command unprecedented sums. Sponsorship revenues continue to expand. Digital platforms have multiplied commercial opportunities across every continent. The World Cup has become one of the most valuable sporting properties ever created.

Where immense and predictable revenue exists, global finance inevitably follows. The same investment logic that transformed airports, infrastructure, healthcare, housing, and media has increasingly reached professional sport. Football is hardly immune. Club ownership has become internationalised. Sovereign wealth funds have entered elite competitions. The proposed restructuring of the World Cup represented the logical extension of that trajectory.

The World Cup has always possessed an unusual legitimacy because its value is collectively created. No investment fund built football’s emotional economy. Its worth emerged through generations of communities playing, supporting, teaching, and preserving the game. Markets can monetise that value. They cannot create it. This distinction lies at the heart of the current debate.

For perhaps the first time in years, football’s governing establishment encountered meaningful resistance to the assumption that every successful institution must eventually submit to the logic of financial markets. This resistance carries significance beyond sport. It demonstrates that institutional choices remain possible even within highly commercialised environments. Not every valuable asset must become a financial product. Not every cultural institution must maximise investor value. Public legitimacy still possesses political force when organisations risk losing the confidence of those they claim to represent. Trust, once weakened, is rarely restored overnight. The deeper challenge facing FIFA is therefore not simply rebuilding consensus among its member associations. It is clarifying what kind of institution it intends to be.

Is it primarily the commercial manager of the world’s most profitable sporting event? Or is it the steward of football’s global public trust? Those identities increasingly point in different directions. The collapse of the private equity proposal offers a temporary reprieve rather than a permanent settlement. Financial markets rarely abandon assets capable of generating billions in future revenue. The pressures to commercialise, restructure, and monetise football’s greatest tournament will almost certainly return in different forms.

The next proposal may look different. The underlying incentives will not. For now, football’s governing bodies have demonstrated that resistance remains possible. They have reminded FIFA that legitimacy cannot be measured only in balance sheets and valuations. That may prove to be the most important lesson of this episode.

Debashis Chakrabarti is a political commentator and Commonwealth Fellow (UK)

editorials.title: Electric transition
editorials.passage:
India’s heavy dependence on imported crude oil remains one of its biggest strategic and economic vulnerabilities. As the world’s third-largest consumer of crude oil, India imports over 90% of its crude oil requirements and consumes around 243 million tonnes of petroleum products annually, resulting in an import bill exceeding $100 billion. Consequently, fluctuations in global oil prices, geopolitical conflicts and currency movements adversely affect India through higher fuel prices, inflation, increased transport costs and pressure on the economy.

Diversifying oil suppliers, maintaining strategic petroleum reserves and blending ethanol with petrol may reduce the risks. But the long-term solution lies in replacing oil with electricity generated from domestic renewable sources.

Transport is central to this transition. Nearly all petrol and about 70% of diesel in India are used by road transport. Every internal combustion vehicle replaced by an electric vehicle lowers crude oil imports.

Concerns that EVs merely shift emissions from vehicles to coal-fired power plants are becoming less significant as India's electricity sector rapidly expands renewable energy capacity while investing in battery storage, pumped hydro and grid modernisation. Even under the current electricity mix, EVs remain far more energy-efficient than conventional vehicles. As the electricity grid becomes cleaner, EVs become cleaner as well.

Electrification also reshapes India's energy economy by replacing imported fuels with locally-generated energy. Solar parks, wind farms and hydropower stations strengthen national energy independence and reduce exposure to external geopolitical shocks.

The transport sector offers the greatest opportunity for reducing oil dependence. Electric two-wheelers and three-wheelers have already demonstrated the viability of this transition. Since two-wheelers account for over 60% of petrol consumption, widespread adoption can significantly reduce fuel demand. Electric scooters have become attractive primarily because they are cheaper to operate and maintain than petrol vehicles. Similarly, electric rickshaws have expanded rapidly due to their lower operating costs.

Passenger cars represent the next stage. Although their current market share remains modest, falling battery costs and expanding domestic manufacturing under production-linked incentive schemes are steadily bringing EVs closer to cost parity with petrol cars.

Commercial transport offers even greater potential. Heavy trucks consume a disproportionate share of diesel despite forming only a small percentage of the vehicle fleet. Buses transport millions daily. Electrifying these segments yields significant reductions in diesel consumption and emissions. Electric buses, despite higher initial costs, have lower lifetime operating and maintenance expenses because electricity is cheaper than diesel and electric drivetrains have fewer mechanical components. Innovative procurement models, such as public-private partnerships and gross cost contracts, have further improved their financial viability. Replacing diesel buses reduces air and noise pollution as well. The Indian railways, already among the world's largest railway electrification programmes, offers a strong foundation. Shifting more freight from roads to electrified railways reduces diesel consumption, logistical costs and exposure to oil price volatility.

Agriculture still relies heavily on diesel-powered irrigation pumps despite expanding rural electrification. Replacing them with electric or solar-powered pumps lowers farmers' fuel costs while reducing diesel demand. Programmes like PM-KUSUM have demonstrated that solar irrigation can increase farm incomes and reduce dependence on fluctuating fuel prices.

By electrifying transport, agriculture and industry while expanding clean electricity generation, India can substantially reduce its oil dependence, lower import costs, improve air quality and enhance long-term energy security.

Atul Agrawal works at the Indian Institute of Management, Sirmaur

editorials.title: Rocked again: Editorial on India-US ties and Trump's tariff threats
editorials.passage:
The already rocky relations between India and the United States of America are poised for heightened turbulence with Washington ready to impose fresh tariffs on countries that purchase Russian energy. The US president, Donald Trump, signed into law a bill on Saturday that had been pushed by the late Republican senator, Lindsay Graham, under which the White House can impose 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas. The measure is aimed at cutting off Moscow’s economic lifeline amid its war on Ukraine, now into its fifth year. But the law, if enforced, also risks mutilating the carefully constructed and managed ties between India and the US. The ministry of external affairs, in a firm statement issued after both Houses of the US Congress had passed the bill, warned that its implementation could adversely impact relations. For a country with a legacy of weighing each diplomatic word with caution before uttering it, New Delhi’s position is clear: India will choose the sources of its energy based on its calculations and that it would respond to attempts by the US to penalise it by taking steps of its own.

After years of effectively succumbing to US pressure and allowing Washington to dictate who India trades with — Iran, Venezuela and Russia are examples — it is indeed time for New Delhi to draw a line in the sand. Relationships are built on respect. Kowtowing to intimidation only invites more pressure. China has never followed unilaterally imposed US sanctions on other countries. Significantly, even though it imports more Russian oil than India does, Beijing had escaped Mr Trump’s tariffs for purchasing Russian crude last year when he imposed penalties on India. New Delhi must also keep the window open to de-escalate with Washington — ties with the US are of fundamental importance and a trade deal between the two countries is also being worked out. Hearteningly, New Delhi and Washington have the tools to do so. The new law allows exemptions that Mr Trump could invoke in India’s case. New Delhi is already buying more Venezuelan oil than at any point in years — and paying the US for it. It could offer to buy more in exchange for a tariff waiver. The upcoming visit to the US by the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, also gives Mr Trump a diplomatic reason to avoid provoking harsh pushback from major buyers of Russian oil. Diplomacy should be India’s preference; but it must be prepared for an economic battle should Mr Trump thrust it upon New Delhi.

editorials.title: Perilous play: Editorial on Bengal's bizarre bypoll drama
editorials.passage:
There is never a dull moment in Bengal’s politics. This, however, is not being said in mirth. First, the Election Commission of India froze the symbol of the undivided Trinamool Congress for the upcoming bypolls on October 6; the TMC’s two warring factions were allotted alternative identities and signages with the ‘Mamata All India Trinamool Congress’ receiving the emblem of a football player. Next, the candidate of the Mamata Banerjee faction in Nandigram pulled out of the fray after a mysterious meeting with the Bengal chief minister. With no opportunity left to find an alternative, Ms Banerjee was then forced to support the Congress candidate for the seat, but he was put in jail in an old murder case: the latter has been remanded in judicial custody till October 3 by a district court. That was not the final scene in this bizarre poll drama. The MAITC’s candidate in the other seat, Rejinagar in Murshidabad, announced his withdrawal from the contest, only to return to the fight. One of his opponents has alleged that his continuation would facilitate a division in the vote meant for the rivals of the Bharatiya Janata Party.

Is there a method to the madness? That possibility cannot be ruled out. The EC’s controversial decision to freeze the symbol of the TMC — there is a precedent in the form of the trajectory of the Shiv Sena’s fate — will now be tested in court. But even before a judicial verdict, the step would undoubtedly deal a psychological blow to Ms Banerjee’s support base. The Congress candidate’s incarceration has led the BJP’s critics to claim institutional intimidation in a seat that is the chief minister’s home turf. The BJP, unsurprisingly, has denied the charge. All of this would strike Bengal’s electorate as the unfolding of a familiar, dispiriting tale. The electoral turf has never been fair no matter which party has been in power in the state. The political colours have changed but the modus operandi to tweak the poll pitch remains constant. This continuity also enables successive regimes to indulge in whataboutery when faced with the charge of coercion. This cannot be a testament to the claims of change that are in the air in Bengal.

editorials.title: Why it’s time to reset India’s insurance sector
editorials.passage:
Reforms in insurance distribution are a key focus of the ongoing comprehensive review of the regulatory framework by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI). Insurance distribution in India is done mainly through regulated intermediaries, and a central issue is the remuneration paid to them. Historically, the Insurance Act, 1938, imposed statutory limits on these costs paid by direct insurance companies, which were modified from time to time.

These sub limits were removed to provide operational flexibility under the IRDAI Expenses of Management (EOM) Regulations, 2024, subject to an overall cap of 30 per cent on EOM. However, capping this overall limit has not adequately addressed the underlying problems of excessive intermediary payments, aggressive pricing, governance and insufficient transparency.

The insurance industry is a major component of India’s financial system. In FY26, the industry’s annual revenue was approximately ₹13.4 lakh crore, comprising ₹10 lakh crore from life insurance and ₹3.4 lakh crore from non-life insurance. Insurance funds are closely connected with banks, capital markets, taxation and government securities, and thus have wider economic and financial-stability consequences.

After the sector opened up in 2000, a few private insurers sought to acquire profitable business and increase volumes by paying higher acquisition costs. Payments were sometimes classified under expenses such as marketing, publicity, printing, travel and information technology, effectively circumventing prescribed limits with differentials across distribution channels. Over the last two decades, aggressive marketing and competition for business became synonymous with rising intermediary remuneration and lower insurance prices across insurance segments.

Penalties for regulatory violations have not been able to create effective deterrence. The new framework being considered by the IRDAI, which according to reports, proposes to relate penalties to the nature and extent of violations, could be an important improvement. Effort-based remuneration and commission caps on specific statutory lines of business, such as motor third-party premium, may also be proposed.

Higher acquisition costs, coupled with lower pricing, is leading a race to the bottom. Recently, the IRDAI cautioned insurers that in the fire portfolio, some insurers were giving 99 per cent discount on standard rates.

Further, the RBI, in its latest Financial Stability Report (June 2026), refers to “a direct financial stability concern” due to the persistent non-compliance to solvency norms by three public sector undertakings from Q4 2024-25 to Q4 2025-26. This is primarily due to sustained underpricing of key portfolios, including group health and high expenses. Net losses piled up to ₹11,400 crore in FY26 (underwriting losses ₹20,267 crore).

Despite a capital infusion of ₹17,450 crore since FY20, additional infusion of capital is required to keep these companies solvent. Estimates vary, inter alia, depending on the plans to sell equity holdings, such as stakes in the NSE, and the proposed change in accounting norms. Some foreign insurers have also found the market difficult. An American insurance major, with 18 years of operations and total capital and share premium of ₹2,704 crore, had an accumulated loss of ₹1,457 crore as on March 31, 2026. A European insurer that commenced operations in 2008 had accumulated losses of ₹1,315 crore by June 2021 prior to being sold.

There is a gap between formal governance systems and actual business practices. Companies file Board-approved policies for all areas of operations with the IRDAI which must be followed diligently. Instances of 9 9 per cent discount on rates or exceedingly high acquisition costs reaching 50-60 per cent point to governance issues.

The (FSDC) Financial Stability and Development Council is the apex-level mechanism for coordination among financial sector regulators. The RBI can share the direct and indirect payments received by all regulated entities (banks and NBFCs) from insurers over 10 years. SEBI can re verify data in public issues with the IRDAI.

Information concerning intermediaries, claims, legal disputes, pricing and investments in the sector can assist in regulatory decision-making.

Intermediaries: Publish data on intermediaries and their associates who receive payments from insurers, directly or indirectly, in any form. It will also highlight concentration risk in the general insurance market. A IBAI McKinsey report indicates that 10 out of 462 brokers control 70 per cent of the market.

Claims: Disclose the portfolio-wise number and value of claims repudiated by insurers and pending legal cases. Analysis across all insurance portfolios could reveal patterns of disputes and help assess the industry’s trust deficit. Pricing data on major corporate property and group health insurance premiums and claims over a 10-year period, together with intermediary-related expenses, will help identify persistent under-pricing.

The Insurance Information Bureau (IIB) and insurance councils can assist with relevant data. Investments data on incremental investments in government securities and other approved investments should be monitored, rather than focusing only on gross investment figures. This will highlight insurers’ cash flows and the yearly surplus available for investments. It is pertinent to note that even 25 years after the sector opened up, LIC’s investments represented about 73.3 per cent (₹54.52 lakh crore to ₹74.4 lakh crore) of the industry’s total investments/AUM as of March 2025.

The IRDAI Annual Report Furnishing of Returns Rules, set up in 2000, must be recast with data and analysis to reflect all issues with brokers, corporate agents, web aggregators, online channels, along with GST and funds flow in the current integrated financial system. IPOs and private equity inadequate disclosure has enabled valuation arbitrage on account of information asymmetry. The proposed regulatory reforms, together with Ind AS accounting and risk-based solvency requirements, could help bring valuations closer to underlying fundamentals.

Stronger governance, comprehensive public data, transparent intermediary payments, better claims reporting and risk-sensitive solvency standards are essential for the insurance sector to make a substantially greater contribution to economic growth over the next two decades.

The writer is a senior insurance professional
