editorials.title: Data centres must be taxed properly
editorials.passage:
Politicians, entrepreneurs, mathematicians, scientists and computer programmers are all starting to complain about the artificial intelligence revolution. They think it will kill us all quite soon.

Economists are quiet, however. That’s a great pity because they can illuminate the dilemmas very clearly and provide a guide towards sensible and practical policy.

The issue can actually be summed up in one sentence. Until now machines displaced manual labour but now they will displace brain work. It’s labour substitution by capital.

The problem now, however, is that whereas the old machines couldn’t link up with each other and take decisions without human prompting, the new computing machines can. And they are much faster than humans.

There’s only one reason they can do so: the availability of massive amounts of data about everything and anything under the sun. They process it at unbelievable speeds.

In other words, data are to computers what a bullet is to a gun or petrol is to a car or butter is to toast. One is useless without the other.

Economics calls them complementary goods. The demand for such goods move up or down together, like whiskey and salted peanuts.

This joint characteristic should underlie the direction of protective policies against AI. If the world stopped collecting data on such a huge scale, and it is truly huge, the computing threat of the machines would be severely diminished.

The policy question then is how much data should be permitted to be collected — if at all indeed the activity of data collection can be controlled. But given that it can’t, because the process is automatic now, the regulatory problem comes down to access to the data.

This is what the EU has been trying to address in the first instance. Controls on the use of that data comes next.

In a nutshell, then, the AI threat issue is about policies towards complementary goods. And governments the world over have used taxation of one to reduce consumption of the other — example, cars and petrol, tobacco and smoking or uranium and nuclear weapons, and so on.

Economists, the real ones from the past, have examined the link between taxes and complementary goods extensively. There is one basic consideration that has emerged, namely, cross price elasticity.

It measures how much the demand for something changes when the price of a complementary good changes. This, by the way, is taught in the first term of the first year of an economics course.

Anyway, the thing is this: if you tax one and it leads to a fall in demand for both, not just one, you need to rethink the rates because this could lead to a drop in revenue from both. The rates, therefore, play a crucial role if the policy is to alter the demand for one of the goods via taxes. That’s standard economic theory.

But India, in its wisdom, far from taxing them, has given data centres a 20-year tax holiday on the condition that they use an Indian partner! So if an American company hires an Indian data centre in India for storing data of its US clients, it gets a tax holiday just for that part of the data. This sounds innocuous but in practice is a huge concession.

That’s why if you are worried about AI this is absolutely the wrong policy. But if, like Donald Trump, you aren’t, then you need to stop talking about regulations because you can’t have both zero taxes and implementable regulation.

The emphasis is on the term implementable and a tax would have been highly implementable. And we are very good at that “if it moves, tax it” sort of approach.

Meanwhile, no country has been able to figure out a workable way of regulating AI because it’s not technologically possible. Whatever you do, the machines and their companies are smart enough to figure out a way of working around the regulations without becoming legally liable.

So where does that leave us? Basically, with no or little taxation and poor regulatory capacity, we are at the mercy of self-propelling algorithms and profit driven companies.

It is tempting to hark back to that wonderfully prescient novel by Arthur C Clarke in which, as far back as 1962, he talks about a computer aboard a spaceship that goes rogue and starts killing the crew. In the end there is only one option left to the one crew member left alive. He turns off its power.

Realistically speaking that’s the only option if safety is the dominant concern because it’s not AI that is the problem but some part of it going rogue even if only in a very minor way. And what’s the probability of that? That’s like asking if there’s life in the universe other than on earth.

Published on September 22, 2026

editorials.title: Compressed biogas can strengthen energy security
editorials.passage:
As mounting US sanction pressures on oil imports threaten India’s energy security, the Cabinet’s recent approval of the Galvanizing Organic Bio-Agro Resources Dhan (GOBARdhan) scheme — backed by an ₹23,731 crore outlay through FY 2035-36 — could not be more timely. Compressed biogas (CBG), purified from organic waste to over 90 per cent methane, could substitute CNG in vehicles — as with Indore’s 400 CBG buses — or be injected into city gas networks for homes and industries.

India’s surplus organic waste has an estimated annual CBG potential of 40-60 million tonnes, enough to meet almost all of the country’s domestic natural gas demand and reduce increasingly costly LNG imports. More than 10 States, including Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh, have also notified CBG or bioenergy policies in the last five years.

But capital alone will not suffice. The Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation (SATAT) scheme, for instance, launched in 2018, envisaged 5,000 CBG plants across India. But only around 217 have been commissioned. High upfront costs, difficult biomass logistics, and weak fermented organic manure (bio-slurry) offtake constrained projects. GOBARdhan must use this opportunity to correct these operational gaps.

First, State governments should institutionalise feedstock pricing. A CBG plant is only as reliable as its biomass supply. Research by the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW) shows that inconsistent feedstock quality and unpredictable prices constrain capacity utilisation, while dispersed, ad hoc crop residue collection makes aggregation costly.

Along with notified CBG policies, States should create transparent pricing mechanisms that keep feedstock affordable for plants while giving farmers a fair return. Precedents already exist. In 2025, the Commission for Air Quality Management directed Punjab and Uttar Pradesh to mandate a common determined rate for paddy straw procurement, following Haryana’s lead. State energy development agencies should undertake price-discovery studies with research institutions and industry, accounting for collection, transport and storage costs. A credible range could keep feedstock affordable for plants without hurting farmers.

Second, State governments should invest in decentralised, secure biomass storage. Agricultural residue like paddy straw is seasonal and should be baled during narrow harvest windows for year-round use. Currently, biomass companies lose 15-25 per cent of feedstock annually due to improper storage practices, moisture ingress, and fires. Storing 10,000 tonnes of bales requires 7-10 acres, while companies keep 70-85 per cent of feedstock on leased land outside plant perimeters.

States should facilitate long-term leases near plants and support weatherproofing storage sites through tarpaulins, drainage, and scientific stacking so biomass reaches digesters without degrading. This would require an initial investment of ₹250-400 per tonne of bales.

The Punjab Pollution Control Board, supported by CEEW, is already developing first-of-its-kind biomass storage guidelines for handling and stacking of agricultural bales.

Third, States should allocate feedstock and new plants strategically. India generates around 226 million tonnes of surplus crop residue annually, and burning it is estimated to account for 13 per cent of India’s PM2.5 emissions. But crop-residue burning is not a uniform problem, and treating it as one risks creating stranded CBG assets. States should use a combination of satellite imagery, groundwater data, and end-use demand to identify blocks where CBG plants are suitable.

Public capital support for balers, storage, and transport should be concentrated in areas with abundant residue, low water stress, and nearby CBG demand (say Hisar in Haryana). High stubble areas without nearby buyers should instead prioritise in-situ management, while water-stressed regions (Patiala in Punjab or Kaithal in Haryana) should pursue crop diversification. Such precision ensures new CBG plants are commissioned only where feedstock supply is viable, preventing stranded assets.

Finally, State agriculture departments and CBG producers should establish a reliable market for bio-slurry. Agricultural-residue plants produce biomanure at a feedstock-to-biomanure ratio of 1:2 to 1:2.5, making FOM (fermented organic manure) sales essential to plant profitability, but low farmer awareness remains a barrier. ICAR has already notified application guidelines (dosage, frequency, and methods) for fermented manure. Now State agricultural universities, KVKs and civil societies should partner with governments. Fertilizer public sector undertakings should also support CBG operators with branding, marketing, and distribution.

India is beginning to treat organic waste as an energy-security resource. The next test is execution.

The writer is Programme Lead at the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW). Views are personal

editorials.title: The Graham Bill comes at a wrong time
editorials.passage:
These are difficult times in India-US relations, not that the two nations have not been there before. When President Donald Trump signed into law the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, he set in motion the prospect of imposing tariffs of up to 100 per cent on countries importing Russian oil and gas. It does not mean penalties will kick in immediately, but China and India have been put on notice, the former lapping up one half of Russia’s crude exports followed by India at around 37 percent.

The percentages vary: for instance, this July, Russia supplied more than half of India’s imports, or more than the combined crude purchased from the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Venezuela, Brazil, Oman and the US.

Initially, the White House was a bit reluctant to support the legislation, but became an enthusiastic cheerleader after sponsors agreed to extend sanctions on Iran for another five years. The Bill first cleared the Senate by an overwhelmingly 86-11 vote, followed by a 262-159 majority in the House of Representatives. The Bill, which had a vocal Democratic Senator co-sponsor, Richard Blumental, also sanctions Russian officials, banks and the so-called shadow fleet that keeps crude flowing.

The overwhelming support for the Graham Bill in the House and Senate did not mean lawmakers were without serious reservations about the legislation. The chief concerns were the discretion given to the President in determining which countries would face tariffs, the rates at which they would be imposed, and if total waivers should be given.

Technically, Turkey and Europe should also be worried, but an exception clause allows waivers for countries that import less than 15 per cent and have taken “significant steps” to reduce Russian imports. “Why in the world would this Congress or the People’s House give this President unfettered authority to visit more tariffs on the world that will have an adverse economic impact on the American people?” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries asked.

The legislation, which will take effect on October 18, or 30 days after Trump’s signature, was received on expected lines in Moscow and Beijing, with Russia maintaining that the new sanctions would make it more difficult to seek a settlement to the Ukraine conflict.

To Moscow, this is an “unfriendly step” at a time when there was some light on re-starting the stalled dialogue between Moscow and Kyiv by the visit of President Trump’s special envoys to the warring capitals recently. The Graham legislation also comes at a time when world leaders are set to gather in New York for the annual General Assembly session of the United Nations.

Beijing’s reaction was far more tough, stressing that the new measures had no legal basis and that they contradict international law.

“We always oppose long arm jurisdiction that has no basis in international law or authority of UN Security Council,” said China’s Foreign Ministry. The sanctions Bill also comes at an awkward time for Trump as he readies for the second summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping on September 24-25. Washington is aware that Beijing cannot be easily pressured by threats of tariffs or sanctions, having demonstrated an ability to respond in equal measure by placing export curbs on rare earths. Further, the threat of new levies is when top officials of the two countries are finalising a tariff regime.

India, for its part, has warned of the “potential implications” to bilateral relations, stressing that all necessary measures would be taken to protect its economic interests. Expectedly, New Delhi has said that it “… remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people. It will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics”. With the two nations on the verge of signing a trade deal, there is a fear that Washington could use the Graham Bill to squeeze more out of India by way of concessions.

The writer is a senior journalist who has reported from Washington DC on North America and United Nations

Published on September 22, 2026

editorials.title: An Arctic security bargain
editorials.passage: By Harsh Pant The new US-Denmark-Greenland security agreement marks an important, if uneasy, adjustment in the strategic balance in the Arctic. It expands the US military and investment-screening role in Greenland without altering the island’s formal constitutional status or transferring sovereignty. Announced by President Donald Trump last week, with formal signing expected at the UN General Assembly in New York, subject to parliamentary ratification, it brings an end, for now, to months of extraordinary tension triggered by his repeated suggestions that Washington should acquire or even seize Greenland. ALSO READHow real is India’s growth? The significance of the agreement lies less in any change in sovereignty than in the expansion of the US’ strategic access. Trump has described the arrangement as providing Washington “permanent control over security, and all other needs” through an “‘Infinite Life Agreement”, while insisting that it would come at no cost to the US. The reported provisions point towards a substantial strengthening of the American military position on the island. Washington would gain expanded rights to develop additional bases, maintain permanent access, and exercise broader basing and overflight privileges. This is, however, an extension of existing architecture. The US already operates Pituffik Space Base under the 1951 Defense of Greenland Agreement, which provides Washington with broad, open-ended rights. What the new arrangement does is institutionalise and potentially widen that strategic footprint. The agreement is equally significant for what it seeks to prevent. Non-NATO states — most obviously Russia and China — would be barred from establishing military bases or maintaining a military presence in Greenland, while sensitive investments would require US approval. The investment-screening provisions are particularly revealing. The emerging contest in the Arctic is not simply about military geography; it is also about control over infrastructure, critical minerals, and technological supply chains. Greenland’s mineral wealth, including rare earth elements, has acquired added importance as Western governments seek to reduce dependence on China which dominates rare-earth processing. Yet, the agreement preserves political red lines — Danish sovereignty and the territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark are reaffirmed, while Greenlanders’ right to self-determination remains intact. There is no transfer of territory or ownership; the Danish and Greenlandic leaders have presented the arrangement as a strengthening of Arctic and North Atlantic security rather than a surrender of sovereignty. For Denmark, this distinction is critical. Copenhagen has avoided the far more destabilising possibility of a confrontation with its principal NATO ally over the territorial integrity of the kingdom. Its leaders had warned that the use of force by one NATO member against another would strike at the foundations of the alliance itself. There are tangible advantages for Denmark. Greater US military engagement could strengthen the defence of the Arctic at a time when Denmark itself has been increasing defence spending and regional capabilities. Expanded US activity could also generate economic opportunities. But the arrangement comes with costs. Copenhagen and Nuuk will have less room for manoeuvre over certain categories of foreign investment, particularly where the US determines that Chinese or Russian involvement poses a strategic risk. More importantly, months of political pressure have left behind a degree of distrust that an agreement alone cannot easily remove. Greenland’s position remains particularly delicate. The island, with a population of roughly 56,000, has an extraordinary strategic geography but limited political and economic capacity. Its location makes it critical for missile warning, North Atlantic sea lanes, and emerging Arctic shipping routes, while its mineral resources add an economic dimension to its strategic value. Greenlandic reactions to the agreement have combined relief at the de-escalation with continuing apprehension about the long-term consequences of a much larger American role. The European implications are broader still. The episode exposed a fundamental vulnerability within NATO. US pressure on Denmark forced European governments to contemplate an extraordinary scenario where a NATO ally’s territory became the subject of coercive bargaining by NATO’s leading power. The agreement provides a diplomatic off-ramp from that crisis. NATO can now focus on the more conventional objective of strengthening the defence of the High North and North Atlantic. But the damage to trust may prove more durable than the immediate dispute. European governments have already been moving towards greater defence capabilities and strategic autonomy, and the Greenland crisis reinforces the logic behind those efforts. Thus, the agreement paradoxically strengthens NATO’s northern flank while highlighting the political vulnerabilities within the alliance. It demonstrates that expanded US access can become a mechanism for de-escalation, but it also shows the risks created when the territorial interests of allies become bargaining instruments in a broader strategic negotiation. For the wider Arctic, the deal consolidates a Western security perimeter around one of the region’s most strategically key locations. It limits the space available for Chinese and Russian military or economic penetration while supporting US aims in missile defence and critical-mineral supply chains. At the same time, it is important not to exaggerate the immediate military threat posed by either Beijing or Moscow to Greenland itself. Before the crisis, many American and European officials saw limited direct military threats to the island. The more consequential competition has been over economic access, infrastructure, technology, and political influence. Climate change makes the competition more pertinent. As the Arctic becomes more accessible, its sea routes, resources, and military geography are acquiring greater strategic significance. Greenland sits at the intersection of these trends. Its importance is unlikely to diminish regardless of which government is in power in Washington, Copenhagen, or Nuuk. ALSO READWanted: fresher; 3 years’ experience essential The agreement should be understood as a reconfiguration of Greenland’s strategic context. Trump obtains greater American leverage and a durable security role. Denmark retains sovereignty and Greenland its constitutional and self-determination framework. The underlying lesson is more complicated. Great-power competition is increasingly spilling into spaces once seen as peripheral to mainstream geopolitics. The Arctic is no longer a geographical frontier; it is becoming a central arena in the contest over military access, critical minerals, infrastructure, and strategic influence. Greenland will remain a test of resilience of the transatlantic order. The agreement’s longer-term significance will depend on how the new military access and investment-screening mechanisms are implemented, and on whether Denmark and Greenland conclude that their sovereignty is being strengthened by the deal or gradually constrained by it. The writer is Vice President, Studies and Foreign Policy, Observer Research Foundation, New Delhi. editorials.title: Let’s financially equip gig workers
editorials.passage: By CS Mohapatra & Depannita Ghosh A delivery rider is paid through an app, buys his fuel and sends money home via UPI, and can tell his customer rating to the last decimal. Yet he might only quote what the platform paid him rather than what he makes, and merely guess about any insurance coverage. In other words, he is thoroughly banked, yet unable to comprehend his own finances fully and maximise financial well-being. This gap in India’s gig economy needs policy attention. A National Centre for Financial Education survey found only 27% of Indian adults are financially literate. For a salaried worker, provident fund, insurance, and a payslip absorb much of the financial-management burden. But gig workers need to manage all three themselves. ALSO READAn Arctic security bargain A study by Dvara Research in Bengaluru found platform workers grossing Rs 35,075 a month and spending Rs 18,470 on fuel, maintenance, and other running costs. Most workers perceive the gross income as net. The Economic Survey 2025-26 records about 40% of gig workers earning below Rs 15,000 a month. Of 11 the platforms assessed in the Fairwork India ratings for 2024, only two could evidence workers earning the local minimum wage once costs were deducted. The behavioural evidence supports the financial literacy deficit in gig workers. A study by LEAD at Krea University found 62% lacked emergency fund, and close to half had no insurance. A 2024 survey across 40 cities by Borzo found 65% lacking life insurance, 77% holding no mutual funds, and 61% being unable to state the income tax slabs. Two-thirds of gig workers had never filed a return. Only 20% earned Rs 2.5 lakh to Rs 5 lakh annually. For ride hailing services, while GST is managed by the platform, the workers are supposed to monitor their tax liabilities themselves. Lack of financial knowledge can result in self-inflicted exclusion from credit. It has also become a constraint for existing schemes. The Atal Pension Yojana crossed 900 million gross enrolments in April; it pays Rs 1,000-5,000 a month for those aged 60 years or above. The PM Shram Yogi Maandhan similarly offers Rs 3,000. Registration on e-Shram is now the gateway to labour code protections. Yet by June, against an estimated 12 million gig workers and a Budget commitment to cover roughly Rs 1 crore, the labour ministry put the number registered at between 1 and 1.2 million. Kenya offers a warning signal. By 2024, 84.8% of Kenyan adults had access to formal financial services compared to 26.7% in 2006. However, the FinAccess surveys, held every two to three years, revealed that only 18.3% were financially healthy. Inclusion produces borrowers. India’s instant loan apps are advertising to precisely this demographic. Platforms record every trip, incentive, and deduction. A monthly statement in the worker’s language, setting out gross earnings, work-related costs, and net take-home, would hand millions of people data they currently lack. A worker who can see his net income can plan around it. The government or NGOs can make a short financial capability module a condition for aggregator registration in the workers’ own language. Financial education cannot be an induction exercise; it has to travel alongside working life cycles. Platforms can use short, vernacular, mobile-first modules, interactive simulations, and gamified learning to explain budgeting, insurance, pensions, mutual funds, credit, taxation, and digital fraud. Workers should receive timely nudges when they get an incentive, take a loan, make a large withdrawal, or become eligible for a government scheme, directing them to the regulated financial product or official source. Periodic financial-literacy camps at delivery hubs, transport centres, and gig-worker congregation points, supported by banks, regulators, insurers, and pension providers, can complement in-app learning. Four topics carry the most immediate value: budgeting on an income that changes weekly, the difference between gross and net, how to enrol in a pension and an insurance scheme, and why an instant loan app quoting a daily rate is the most expensive money they will borrow. Gig workers should know the simple difference between a bank deposit, insurance, pension, mutual fund, and credit product; who regulates each of them; how to check if a provider is legitimate; and which government schemes they are eligible for. A “financial toolkit” embedded in every gig platform could provide links to regulated products and official portals, explain eligibility in plain language, and allow workers to compare costs, risks, and benefits before they commit their money. Once workers understand the financial products and schemes available, platforms should use timely nudges. For example, reminding a newly eligible worker to enrol in a pension or insurance plan, or showing the true cost of an instant loan before it is taken. Auto-enrolment in the Atal Pension Yojana at onboarding, with a visible opt-out and the contribution met from the levy aggregators already owe, will enrol more gig workers in a quarter than a decade of awareness campaigns. ALSO READHow real is India’s growth? Financial awareness is worth little if the system cannot see the worker back. India already has the Account Aggregator framework. Platform earnings history should flow into it with the worker’s consent. Besides, literacy surveys can consider carrying a gig worker module as there is no separate national measurement of financial capability. Riders know their rating as it matters to them as well as the platform, but they aren’t aware about what they net in a month. A design choice made by platforms can remove this asymmetry of knowledge. The writers are Respectively IEPF Chair Professor and Senior Research Analyst, National Council of Applied Economic Research, New Delhi. editorials.title: The new playbook for India’s internet economy
editorials.passage: By Karan Taurani For much of the past decade, the internet economy had a fairly simple obsession: growth. Acquire customers, increase orders, expand gross merchandise value (GMV), and wait for scale to deliver profitability. But the latest trends across global technology and commerce companies suggest this playbook is changing. Amazon, Walmart, Alibaba, Meituan, DoorDash, and Instacart are still chasing growth, but the transaction itself is increasingly only the starting point. The bigger opportunity lies in everything that can be built around it. The first change is speed. The lines separating traditional e-commerce, quick commerce, and food delivery are rapidly disappearing. Amazon’s rapid-delivery offering grew around 80%, while Alibaba’s China quick-commerce revenue grew 45% and now accounts for around 20% of group revenue. Alibaba expects non-food to overtake food in instant commerce and has indicated that fast delivery could eventually account for around 30% of platform sales. DoorDash, meanwhile, is moving beyond restaurants and grocery into pharmacy, beauty, wellness, and general merchandise. ALSO READNEET debate is still wide open For India, this changes how we should think about Blinkit and Instamart. The opportunity is no longer merely about taking grocery online and delivering it faster. Once consumers open an app several times a week, and the platform has warehouses and riders positioned close to them, the same infrastructure can potentially serve a much larger part of the consumer wallet. There is, however, an important lesson from China: not every order is equally valuable. PDD has deliberately stayed away from quick commerce, preferring to invest in supply chains and rural demand. During China’s subsidy battle, Meituan found competitive gains were concentrated among mid-to-high-average order value consumers, while more price-sensitive users attracted through competitor subsidies showed weaker repeat behaviour. This is particularly relevant for India. Discounts can buy GMV and market share, but they not necessarily build a valuable consumer franchise. The more profound change, however, is happening after the order is won. Walmart provides perhaps the clearest example. US comparable sales grew just 2.6%, yet profit went up around 10% before tariffs, with almost half of the rise coming from advertising, marketplace, and membership. Walmart’s global advertising revenue grew 38%, Amazon’s ad business grew 26%, while Instacart’s ad revenue rose 16%. This may be the most important global read-through for Indian internet companies. Blinkit, Nykaa, Meesho, Instamart and FirstCry are also potentially powerful media platforms. They know what consumers search for, what they eventually buy, and how frequently they return. Unlike traditional advertising, commerce platforms can close the loop between an advertisement and the final purchase. That means the same consumer and the same GMV can be monetised more than once — potentially at significantly higher margins. Then comes AI, where Indian platforms could occupy an unusually advantageous position. Amazon, Meta, and Alphabet have increased capex sharply as they spend enormous sums building AI infrastructure. Indian consumer platforms do not have to finance that infrastructure race. They can consume the technology that it creates. ALSO READWanted: fresher; 3 years’ experience essential Amazon’s Alexa for Shopping users spend over 40% more per order, while AI-led ad tools are improving conversion and lowering acquisition costs. For Indian platforms, AI can improve search, recommendations, advertising yields, inventory management, customer service, fraud detection, and delivery routing. They could effectively become second-order beneficiaries of the billions of dollars being invested in AI. Automation could eventually address another stubborn cost: fulfilment. DoorDash is experimenting with delivery robots, JD operates autonomous delivery vehicles, and Meituan is scaling drone deliveries. It suggests today’s rider-intensive deliveries shouldn’t be considered the terminal cost structure of these businesses. Put all of this together and the internet playbook is shifting — from maximising GMV to maximising the economics of every customer relationship. The writer is EVP, Elara Capital Disclaimer: The views expressed are the author's own and do not reflect the official policy or position of Financial Express.

editorials.title: Who guards governance?
editorials.passage: The most astounding aspect of the governance controversy at Coforge is not who did what, or even why. It is that the governance architecture of a large listed company could apparently permit one or two individuals — even if they happened to be the chairman and the head of the Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC) — to determine whether material findings from a board peer-review exercise reached the full board. Companies conduct board evaluations precisely to ensure that directors, including the chairman, are subjected to scrutiny. If the person being evaluated can influence whether an unfavourable assessment is seen by fellow directors, the safeguard becomes almost meaningless. It is the corporate equivalent of a schoolchild intercepting a poor report card before it reaches his parents. A credible system cannot depend on an individual voluntarily transmitting information that may reflect adversely on him. It must make suppression or selective circulation of such information structurally difficult. ALSO READHow real is India’s growth? That is why the Coforge episode should not be reduced to a judgement only on OP Bhatt. The more important question is how such discretion was available to any individual in the first place. Sound governance assumes that people have conflicts, biases, and incentives, irrespective of their reputation or intentions. Board evaluations should therefore have an automatic information trail, with the complete report going simultaneously to designated independent directors or the entire board. There should be additional safeguards when the evaluation concerns the chairman or NRC chair. No chairman should have a de facto veto over what fellow directors learn about his evaluation; nor should a committee chair decide unilaterally which findings merit circulation. When governance depends upon the discretion of the person it is supposed to oversee, it ceases to be governance and becomes trust. There is a broader lesson for Indian boardrooms, where governance too often risks becoming synonymous with having distinguished names around the table. Impressive résumés cannot substitute for institutional checks. Boards need to ask some uncomfortable questions after Coforge. Who receives the raw findings of an evaluation? Can management, the chairman, or a committee head edit, summarise, or withhold them? Who ensures that adverse observations concerning the chairman reach independent directors? Is there an audit trail? Shareholder signals matter too. Bhatt’s proposed reappointment did not obtain the required 75% shareholder approval at Coforge’s August annual general meeting. Such dissent should not be dismissed as an inconvenient voting outcome; it is information a board must examine seriously. ALSO READAn Arctic security bargain Coforge deserves credit for subjecting the matter to an internal governance review and subsequently widening its examination of governance processes. But Indian boards should not wait for a controversy to fix an obvious design flaw. Board evaluations may rightly be confidential from outsiders, but not from directors legally and fiduciarily responsible for governing the company. Nor should strong operating performance provide comfort when governance machinery malfunctions: financial performance and governance quality are separate tests. The enduring lesson from Coforge is larger than any chairman, director, or company. Governance is not demonstrated by codes, committees, and annual evaluation exercises, but by whether uncomfortable information can travel through an organisation without being stopped by the people whom it makes uncomfortable. If a listed company’s governance framework leaves room for the corporate equivalent of hiding the report card, the bigger problem is not merely who hid it. It is that the system allowed it to be hidden at all.

editorials.title: There is a racism and cohesion crisis in Britain, and someone needs to lead us out of it. His name is Andy Burnham
editorials.passage:
“T he speech” may have been in the making a long while, maybe for a lifetime, but Andy Burnham has only a week left for revision before his first conference as Labour leader. Expect hope, of course, that the future will be better, though the way is hard. Already his optimism means that fewer people think they will be worse off next year . But his most urgent task is the cultural wildfire that needs extinguishing before it takes hold.

The rise of anti-migration neofascism is more threatening than anything I’ve seen in my lifetime. Shock tactics by a few hundred people in black shirts and balaclavas are designed to invade the national consciousness, their noxious hate bleeding into the mainstream – and they do.

Keir Starmer began well, hosing down the summer 2024 rioters with rapid arrests. But since then, the truth is that Labour has looked ambivalent in challenging aggressive St George’s flag-raisers, and the asylum hotel protesters who claim to be “protecting” the country whose values they are trashing. At the same time, the self-proclaimed patriots of GB News, the Mail, the Telegraph and Elon Musk’s X pump out daily hate of the country. Burnham’s task is to face them down with top-level leadership, and the sheer force of his positivity.

It won’t be easy. Nick Lowles, the founder of the advocacy group Hope Not Hate, says the cordon sanitaire that once defended democratic politics from the far right and ethno-nationalist thuggery is gone. He has patrolled that line all his working life, and now he’s alarmed about the feeble responses from mainstream politicians to the swelling ranks of racist demagogues intent on wrecking what is, still, a remarkably cohesive multicultural society.

But Lowles is encouraged by his latest talks with Downing Street. “They are ready to push back,” he says. “Good people need to stand up.” Keep immigration policy separate, is his advice. “It’s not binary, people want the small boats stopped – but they value the cohesive communities they live in.”

Burnham of the north, immune to the rightwing branding of southerners as “woke”, is the right man to speak plainly against racism to the “red wall” tendency. There is a decency argument to be made. Look how the best-of-British RNLI had to close a station as volunteers were threatened for risking their lives for anyone in peril on the sea. Consider the truth that only 1.2% of RNLI’s emergency launches involve refugees.

Consider that when Sagal Abdi-Wali, once a Somali child refugee and now a local council leader, the Labour candidate for Holborn and St Pancras, a respected public servant, faces ferocious abuse for seeking to serve the public, it’s a direct threat to democracy.

When a poll indicates that 37% of men between 25 and 34 like Tommy Robinson, there can be no doubt that the sewer of hate and misogyny, operating via dark algorithms, needs to be checked, not protected as “free speech”. When tax-exile billionaire Jim Ratcliffe opines from Monaco that immigration and taxes are destroying the country, it’s for Labour to be the patriots who rebut him.

Things are bad when the former prime minister Rishi Sunak, born and bred in the UK, feels obliged, as he did in the Sunday Times at the weekend , to defend his right to be brown and British. Calling himself a beneficiary of “the world’s most successful multi-faith, multi-ethnic democracy”, he was shocked by footage of “someone referring to me as a ‘Paki’ and others questioning the Englishness of a ‘brown Hindu’”. He insisted: “We cannot allow race to be reintroduced into our politics … they are trying to turn Britishness into a DNA test.”

Ed Davey of the Liberal Democrats sees it as his “moral responsibility to stop Reform”, as it is for Labour, and should be for traditional Tories. But Westminster has been muted. When Nigel Farage first announced he would deport 600,000 people, including children, Labour – like the Tories – only opposed his scheme’s cost and impracticality.

Deporting whichever migrants Farage targets next may appeal to some, but it’s for Labour to spell out what that midnight knock would come to mean – not just for millions as British as Sunak, but for us all, with our liberties diluted, and division and hate concentrated.

The tempting counterattack is more hate: knuckle-dusters against knuckle-draggers. But that’s not the right way, says Lowles, who has himself been the target of violence and death threats. His organisation seems to be carrying a lot of the burden here. It’s scrutiny of that dark world – infiltrating and exposing the extremism, gathering names and evidence when violence has been planned – that has prevented outrages and saved lives. The police appear to know far less.

Hope Not Hate, which relies on donations, runs community groups in places at risk of tensions. In mainly white areas of Bradford, Gateshead, Sunderland and elsewhere, it offers free meals in school holidays and provides food banks to bring people together to talk community politics. When racist trouble breaks out anywhere, “we try to get there within 24 hours, to bring together local faith groups and local mothers who don’t want violence,” Lowles says. “Calming down, not countering hate with hate.”

In a world where Trumpites and our own extremists own the loudhailers, his remedy lies with community groups, knowing your neighbours, joining up, being active. He offers reassuring polling : 53% of British adults like “living in a community with people who come from different backgrounds”.

A reflection of that better Britain is what he expects from Labour next week, and so do I. Go on chasing down small boats (arrivals are 41% down this year), but also celebrate the country we live in, protect its social success against opportunistic pedlars of hate.

In my lifetime, I’ve seen what I thought was overt racism made untenable: just watch the toe-curling TV sitcoms of yesteryear. In 2005 Michael Howard, the then Tory party leader, bombed with his shameless dog-whistle campaign slogan, “Are you thinking what we’re thinking?”. No, good people were not.

Those people are still there; the challenge is having the credibility and the will to speak for and to them. Burnham can do that. Next week he should.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

This article was amended on 22 September 2026. In an earlier version, an image showing counter-protesters from Stand Up to Racism was incorrectly captioned as showing the “South Coast Patriots” group.
