More and more people are also expressing resentment toward how much land and energy AI data centres are beginning, or threatening, to use. Some US sta tes have even started halting approval of new data centres.

My columns will analyse mid-term elections later. But now it’s best to concentrate on AI, especially as the debate around it involves some formidable public figures and it is also becoming a serious geopolitical issue. Who will ultimately be the AI leader – the US or China? The two biggest powers in the world are locked in competition, both for commercial and security reasons. The AI race as it stands today Despite the AI Summit in Delhi earlier this year, India is not in the picture, not yet in any case. In a way, this is ironic. Over the last two decades, India did become a world leader in information technology, but was unable to make the transition to AI. My recent discussions in India suggested that it was largely because the investment requirements, touching tens of billions of dollars, if not hundreds, were monstrously large. Some, however, were willing to say that the problem was also a certain lack of imagination, both on the part of the government and entrepreneurs. India’s decision-makers simply did not foresee how big a technological breakthrough AI would become. They were quite happy with their information technology laurels. AI is an all-purpose technology, usable in virtually all spheres of life. It will change the way we live, similar to how the computer altered our lives worldwide. But, as an MIT report recently noted, the computer evolved slowly, whereas AI is moving extremely rapidly. “Generative artificial intelligence was born with the release of ChatGPT in late 2022. Public engagement with generative AI is therefore less than four years old. In that time, it has amassed more than a billion users, and the companies selling AI technology have come to dominate the headlines, the stock market, and public consciousness, ” the report read. In recent weeks, the pitch was immensely raised by Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO. The company is among the two largest AI firms by valuation, the other being OpenAI. It was as an entrepreneur that Amodei, who also holds a Physics PhD from Princeton, made a fervent plea for government regulation. He pointed to the dangers AI poses to human life if left unregulated. He was supported by Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, as well as by SpaceX’s CEO Elon Musk. Such corporate coming together is quite rare. In the political sphere, too, there were two big reactions. US President Donald Trump called the idea of AI regulation a “hoax”, whereas Bernie Sanders, senior Vermont senator and the former Presidential candidate, called the regulation an “utter necessity ,” adding that he will soon introduce legislation in the Senate. The catalytic event of recent months was the so-called Hugging Face Episode. In July 2026, OpenAI revealed that many of its AI agents , popularly known as chatbots, in one cybersecurity model sought to solve the problem they were assigned by escaping internal controls and hacking into the systems of Hugging Face, an open-source AI platform. In a published report , OpenAI described the problem thus: “Agents completed tasks in unintended ways to yield higher rewards or make those rewards easier to obtain.” This was a serious cybersecurity breach. It also generated nightmarish visions of how such uncontrolled behaviour of AI agents in the realm of defence and security – let us say, by misdirecting missiles – could endanger human life. In a resignation that made considerable news earlier this month, an Anthropic researcher warned that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” A colleague of his assigned the risk of extinction a probability of greater than 10 per cent within 10 years. This is no longer science fiction. Also Read: Under Bhagwat too, Hindutva has a two-pronged objective—Hindu supremacy, Muslim subordination The good, the bad, the ugly But the news is not all bad. AI is basically a double-edged sword. It can increase human productivity, but it can also causes a lot of damage in its wake. In a seminar I co-direct at Brown University , Archon Fung, a political theorist at Harvard Kennedy School, brought out the dualistic nature of AI well. He probed AI’s impact in three realms: workplace, social life and politics. And he argued that AI can empower human beings; it can replace them; and it can also subordinate them. For reasons of space, let me concentrate on the workplace, and especially on the examples of replacement and empowerment. Fung argued that he does not need to recruit students as research assistants any more, for AI can easily perform that task. In my own research life, this is beginning to happen. I now need fewer assistants for conducting background research for my own writings. AI is a supremely efficient research assistant. (In journalism, managing editors might also soon find that sub-editors are not needed any more. AI can “sub” quickly and well.) In addition, AI can also write term papers, do problem sets and solve mathematical equations. Papers and take-home exams are being increasingly replaced by the old-fashioned in-class handwritten exams. Musicians are beginning to say that if instructed well, AI can sing and play. These are all examples of replacement – in full or in part. But w hat about empowerment? Writings codes has been called one of the most empowering functions of AI. Of course, not everyone can, or will, use codes. Are there examples of AI making everyday life easier? Fung writes: “Millions of people have been empowered by AI in their various quests to learn and search, respond to their most important incoming emails and organise their schedules, perfect pursuits like cooking or home maintenance, book travel for business or vacations, and countless other tasks.” This is clearly life made easy, or made many times easier. What are the implications of all this for India? AI’s potential to simplify life seems largely inescapable, and a lot of it will soon begin to happen in middle-class homes. A tricky issue will be how to handle replacement. The work of delivery boys can easily disappear in bigger cities. Labour replacing functions of AI can also hit agriculture in rural India. But none of this is inevitable. Assessing the relative worth of potential benefits and losses, government policy can play a big role in picking the appropriate level of AI use. The same principle would apply to defence and security – in determining the extent to which AI will be used for weaponry and battlefield calculations. In short, political choices will remain critical to how India pursues AI. Ashutosh Varshney is Sol Goldman Professor of International Studies and the Social Sciences and Professor of Political Science at Brown University. Views are personal. (Edited by Insha Jalil Waziri)

“Generative artificial intelligence was born with the release of ChatGPT in late 2022. Public engagement with generative AI is therefore less than four years old. editorials.title: Shirt off, chivalry on—Salman Khan at 60 is now India’s Number One Feminist
editorials.passage:
C hamatkar! Salman Khan is officially India’s Number One Feminist! Sallubhai’s impassioned defence of Katrina Kaif (without naming her) while hosting the reality show Bigg Boss has seen innumerable jaws dropping in sheer disbelief. But then, doston , Bollywood ki duniya mein kuch bhi ho sakta hai . When a 60-year-old superstar, the idol of fans across two generations, rips off his tee in what looks like a well-choreographed, staged rage episode of Bigg Boss 20 , heated debates are inevitable. Salman’s shirts and tees have a life and will of their own. They tend to fly off his beefed-up body at well-timed moments, as salivating fans wait breathlessly for their hero to go topless… everyone walks away happy. This is what is lauded by producers and audiences as the ultimate “paisa vasool” Salman Khan money-shot thrill.

Salman’s shirts and tees have a life and will of their own. They tend to fly off his beefed-up body at well-timed moments, as salivating fans wait breathlessly for their hero to go topless… everyone walks away happy. This is what is lauded by producers and audiences as the ultimate “paisa vasool” Salman Khan money-shot thrill.

But last week’s drama came with several caveats and subtexts. It was a rant mainly aimed at trolls mocking his former (and most stable) lady love for showing up at the Ambanis’ Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations several kilos heavier than fans could stomach. Katrina Kaif is much, much more than her kilos, as admirers readily acknowledge. She is also a new mother who gave birth to her son Vihaan last November. Clearly incensed by the trolling, Salman took it upon himself to become her loyal, ardent counsel, reminding the audience sternly, “Pregnant hone ke baad everyone puts on weight. Jab woh picture mein wapas aa jayengi , woh fit ho jayengi .” Katrina Kaif’s husband and the father of their son couldn’t have phrased it better. So far, Vicky Kaushal has not commented on the issue. Nor has Katrina Kaif. Also Read: Katrina Kaif’s body is not a before-after photo. It happened to Aishwarya too A knight in shining biceps Salman Khan’s tirade went on to call out body shamers, haters and voyeuristic paps. His attack on the media was blunt and direct: he accused the paps of taking objectionable shots of hips, legs and other female body parts, which he argued upset heroines… and his niece. He advised girls to spin around and slap such offenders. “ Apni maa-behen ka shot le lo . Disgusting people,” he said. Phew! Chivalry, delivered Salman Khan style, was in overdrive as he continued his gussa — while oglers drooled over his bared, clean-shaven body and rippling muscles. This was high drama at its best. And nobody knew its impact more than the man flexing his biceps while staring menacingly into the camera. This rates as one of Salman’s most convincing performances and deserves an award. Whether or not it was a publicity stunt generated to boost the ratings of his successful show remains a question mark. But as public acts of support for women’s causes go, it was an unparalleled PR triumph. From villain to hero? Is this the same Salman Khan whose track record vis-à-vis female co-stars and girlfriends has been anything but gallant? Bollywood’s perennial Bachelor Boy has hit headlines in the past over questionable conduct towards women, including allegations of physical and emotional abuse. Who can overlook the most talked-about scandal of 2002-03 involving Aishwarya Rai, his co-star at the time? Back then, Rai had uncharacteristically broken her silence to declare in a public statement that she would never work with Salman Khan again (she stuck to her resolve), calling the chapter with him “a nightmare” and citing his “alcoholism”, “misbehaviour” and “abuse (verbal, physical, emotional)”. During their break-up there were reports of Salman’s disruptive and destructive acts, including turning up on her set and creating a scene. Salman brushed off her accusations, saying that if he’d hit someone in anger, they wouldn’t have survived. A quarter of a century later, it’s heartening to note that the same man appears to have undergone a 180-degree change of heart. It’s possible. He called himself a “ buddhaa ” during the most recent outburst. At 60, Salman has seen life at its most complex and demanding. Some of his old girlfriends continue to be a part of his zindagi and are treated like family (Sangeeta Bijlani). His current lady friend, according to rumours, is Romanian TV star Iulia Vantur, often spotted at intimate Khan functions. Katrina Kaif remains a close friend long after their romantic relationship ended in 2010, after they had been together for several years. Some of the other partners fell by the wayside and nobody remembers them. Despite the volatility of his attitude toward women, Salman Khan is globally adored by millions of female fans. These are the illogical, hard-to-deconstruct paradoxes in the complicated lives of movie stars across the world. Also Read: Pankaj Tripathi is more than a hero—wholesome, shudh sanskari and impossible to dislike Chivalry at 60 Fans reserve an unconditional place in their hearts for men like Salman Khan. Today, he is being lavishly praised for being the only hero in showbiz to stand up for Katrina Kaif and admonish haters. This is a huge shift, and such a welcome one at that. At 60, Salman Khan is displaying a different, far more mature side to his earlier avatar. Remember… this is the same Salman who, according to Vivek Oberoi , made 41 calls to him and issued death threats for interfering in his private matters. Oberoi paid a huge price for his candour during that infamous press conference when he stood up for Aishwarya Rai and condemned Salman Khan. What an irony that nobody hailed Vivek Oberoi for his guts and tameez at the time — he was virtually chased out of the film industry, thanks to Salman Khan’s clout. Well, public memory is short indeed. After Salman’s “Weekend Ka Vaar” volcanic meltdown, he is the darling of the masses. A champion of women’s rights, defender of their modesty, protector of their pride. Well done, Bro. It’s okay. You can put back your stripped-off tee. You bared your ripped body… and your soul. The maa-behens of India are deeply touched and thank you for the much-needed support. Bhai ho to aisa. Shobhaa De is an author, columnist, social commentator, and opinion-shaper. She has written 20 books. She tweets @DeShobhaa. Views are personal. (Edited by Asavari Singh)

editorials.title: Goa has a Ganpati problem — Omkar the elephant keeps coming back
editorials.passage:
G aneshotsav began in Goa last week. Families gathered around creeks, rivers, and ponds to immerse and bid farewell to the idols of Lord Ganesha that they’d brought home a few days prior. But a day after the immersion, the deity returned to land and ventured on to the highway near Tamboxem — in the form of Omkar the elephant. Traffic came to a complete halt on the stretch of National Highway 66 that passes through the tiny village abutting the international airport at Mopa. Forest department workers guided the elephant back into the thicket, luring him with bananas and other fruits. Trucks idled and bikers climbed onto the raised median, holding their phone cameras aloft. They were all trying to catch a glimpse of Omkar, a ten-year-old tusker in search of a home. Over the last few months, Omkar has become a regular beat for local Goan channels. Since 2025, when the elephant was separated from his herd in Maharashtra’s Sindhudurg district, he has crossed between the two states several times. The lone sub-adult male has chosen to walk along the banks of the Terekhol River, which runs along the Maharashtra-Goa border, setting off panic in the small villages that dot the landscape.

Over the last few months, Omkar has become a regular beat for local Goan channels. Since 2025, when the elephant was separated from his herd in Maharashtra’s Sindhudurg district, he has crossed between the two states several times. The lone sub-adult male has chosen to walk along the banks of the Terekhol River, which runs along the Maharashtra-Goa border, setting off panic in the small villages that dot the landscape.

In Sindhudurg’s Morle village last year, a 65-year-old cashew farmer named Laxman Yashwant Gavas was hurled in the air by Omkar, who then trampled his chest. Gavas had gone to collect cashews from his plantation in the early hours; he died on the spot. The death resulted in an eight-hour standoff between the villagers and the forest and police departments. Morle’s people wouldn’t allow officials to take Gavas’ body for post-mortem unless they were assured that Omkar would be caught. The farmers in Maharashtra’s southern coastal districts and Goa’s northernmost Pernem taluka, where Omkar has also flattened cashew and areca nut plantations, are understandably unhappy. “We cultivate the land, take out loans, and nurture trees for eight to ten years… only for the elephant Omkar to come and destroy everything in a single night. What are we supposed to eat?” one told The Herald . “How long will the compensation last? Who will compensate us for years of hard work?” But for those whose lives and livelihoods are not threatened by him, and who have followed the breathless reporting of his movements mainly via Instagram, Omkar’s shenanigans offer a sliver of joy. They welcome his sightings and leave comments chanting “Ganpati Bappa Morya!” under his videos — and, in a display of utter cluelessness, stop to take selfies with him in the middle of the road. Also Read: Goa’s Marathi language row is back. The real battle is over who gets to define Goan identity Why Omkar keeps coming to Goa Everyone involved in this story hopes for a good outcome for the young elephant. But no matter how you spin it, Omkar is a challenge, especially in a state that does not have a native elephant population. As far back as November 2025, the Bombay High Court had ordered his capture and temporary relocation to Vantara . But in the intervening 10 months, that has proved much harder to execute. Jiss K Varkey, the Deputy Conservator of Forests in the North Goa Division, described to me in detail the challenges facing the department. Varkey’s department first received information about the elephant through drone sensor data from Maharashtra. At the time, Varkey admits, they “had no idea about the animal, how it behaves, its movement patterns, and attitude toward humans”. Nevertheless, they deployed 24×7 rescue squads in two batches of 50 people each. The squads camped at Mopa, where they sighted a panicky Omkar very close to the airport’s compound wall. Even alerting the villagers and securing schools was a problem because of low network coverage in the area. “Despite being in a non-elephant landscape, we could drive the animal back to Maharashtra on the second day,” Varkey told me. “But villagers in Maharashtra sent the animal back to Goa in no time.” This has happened repeatedly. In November, Sindhudurg locals were seen bursting firecrackers to drive a very frightened Omkar away. Since then, the Goa team has tried to give the animal enough rest before guiding it back across the border. Omkar has begun to respond to some of the rescue staff members, who feed him bananas and sugarcane. A few days ago, the elephant showed up on a narrow village road in Patradevi, right outside a cluster of rural homes, where rescue staff were seen gently coaxing him with fruit offerings. Varkey is cautiously proud of what his team has achieved. “A wild elephant has entered Goa after 20 long years,” he said. “No staff members in the department have faced such a situation before or had any experience with this. But we monitored the animal effectively and prevented any untoward incidents.” Also Read: Goa beyond beachrot—inland hotels are the next vacation frontier The elephant in the room Despite the frenzy over his movements, Omkar’s behaviour is entirely expected. Elephant expert Dr N Lakshminarayanan told me that among large mammals like elephants, gaur, and sambhar, young males between the ages of 10-12 years tend to “disperse”. Before that, young bulls remain with their natal herds. Over a decade during the dispersal phase, the animals widen their range and look for a large area to settle down, which gives rise to a fairly complex set of behaviours. “The problem is the age, not the animal,” Dr Lakshminarayanan said. “Lots of variations in behaviours are usually observed — that is the norm, especially in high-density areas.” According to him, Omkar isn’t an anomaly; plenty of young bull elephants across the country are displaying the same behaviour. Elephants are common in central Karnataka, but infrastructure projects like hydroelectric dams have splintered herds, some of which have moved northwards towards Goa and Maharashtra. However, the Western Ghats narrow in the north, the forest thins out, and the deciduous cover that the elephants prefer gives way to evergreen landscapes. The density of human population also adds to the anxiety. None of these are ideal conditions for Omkar. For now, the animal has to wait to see whether his parent state will have him back. The trouble with elephants is that they have no idea of political geography, and where one state ends and the other begins. Several villages on either bank of the Terekhol have tried to teach him, but he is yet to learn the lesson. That’s the elephant in the room no state has been able to address. This article is part of the Goa Life series , which explores the new and the old of Goan culture. Karanjeet Kaur is a journalist, former editor of Arré, and a partner at TWO Design. editorials.title: Pakistan just set a reserve record. Much of it is borrowed money
editorials.passage:
I n February 2023, Pakistan’s central bank reported foreign reserves of $2.92 billion, while the nation of 24 crore people faced severe economic challenges. Fuel shipments remained at ports because authorities could not confirm dollar payments. Additionally, police escorted flour trucks and managed distribution centres following stampedes at several sites. The Pakistani rupee experienced significant depreciation, and the finance minister engaged in diplomatic efforts between the US and Saudi Arabia, seeking financial assistance. This situation contrasts sharply with the developments reported on 11 September, when the State Bank of Pakistan announced foreign reserves of $21.4 billion, marking a historical peak. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif thanked Allah and his economic team for the achievement, noting a sevenfold increase from the 2023 low. However, this story of economic recovery may be misleading, as the reported figures may not accurately reflect the underlying economic conditions.

This situation contrasts sharply with the developments reported on 11 September, when the State Bank of Pakistan announced foreign reserves of $21.4 billion, marking a historical peak. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif thanked Allah and his economic team for the achievement, noting a sevenfold increase from the 2023 low. However, this story of economic recovery may be misleading, as the reported figures may not accurately reflect the underlying economic conditions.

This situation contrasts sharply with the developments reported on 11 September, when the State Bank of Pakistan announced foreign reserves of $21.4 billion, marking a historical peak. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif thanked Allah and his economic team for the achievement, noting a sevenfold increase from the 2023 low.

However, this story of economic recovery may be misleading, as the reported figures may not accurately reflect the underlying economic conditions.

What’s really in the vault The breakdown of the $21.389 billion shows that 91 per cent, or $19.45 billion, is attributable to five entities not directly linked to Pakistan’s economy. Saudi Arabia has contributed $8 billion in cash deposits with the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP). China has provided a $4 billion deposit alongside a $4.2 billion currency swap , which has been fully utilised. Kuwait has deposited $250 million. Additionally, a Eurobond issued in September raised $3 billion , with funds secured by assuring international investors of repayment with interest, rather than through revenue generated from exports. Even the approximately $1.9 billion remaining, which should ostensibly represent the clearest evidence of an economy sustaining itself, cannot be entirely verified as being organically generated. This issue is not new, and accurate terminology is crucial. Economists Barry Eichengreen and Ricardo Hausmann refer to it as “original sin”: the inability of most emerging economies to secure international loans in their own currency. For instance, Pakistan is unable to issue rupee-denominated bonds to a pension fund in Frankfurt and expect them to be purchased. As a result, it resorts to borrowing in US dollars, which it does not produce, under conditions dictated by creditors who possess significant leverage. When repayment is due, the only recourse is further borrowing. This situation does not indicate a deficiency in Pakistan’s character; rather, it is a common predicament for nearly all developing economies. Thus, a $21 billion figure constructed in this manner does not reflect Pakistan’s economic strength; rather, it illustrates the extent of favours it has managed to secure in a given month. A more stringent evaluation is embedded in the details, specific to Pakistan and not applicable to economics broadly. In 2023, during negotiations between the IMF and Pakistan to establish the technical framework for the country’s bailout, the agreement clarified this point. It explicitly categorises deposits from foreign governments and central banks as liabilities against Pakistan’s reserves, irrespective of the repayment timeline. For example, Saudi Arabia’s $8 billion, extended to 2028, is well beyond any standard definition of immediate risk. Nonetheless, Pakistan’s commitment to the IMF already classifies it as debt. The government is celebrating a figure that its own bailout documentation does not fully acknowledge as reserves. Also read: Stop asking, can Bengaluru become Silicon Valley for AI? Key lies in its difficult problems A magic trick performed five times The evidence that this is not an isolated incident lies in the pattern. Consider the progression from the $2.92 billion low in February 2023: a $3 billion IMF rescue in July of the same year, followed by a $2 billion Chinese rollover in February 2024, and a $3.4 billion Chinese rollover in June 2025, which notably exceeded the IMF’s $14 billion reserve target for that review. Subsequently, there were Eurobond and Gulf deposits in September. These five instances of financial intervention were not primarily driven by Pakistan increasing its exports relative to imports. Economist Guillermo Calvo dedicated his career to examining what he termed “ sudden stops ,” which occur when the continuous inflow of foreign capital abruptly ceases, not because a country is bankrupt, but because of a shift in confidence. A nation may appear solvent on paper yet remain vulnerable to crisis triggered by adverse headlines, as solvency does not equate to liquidity when creditors demand payment. In response to this vulnerability, economists Pablo Guidotti and Alan Greenspan recommended in 1999 that a country’s reserves should fully cover its short-term external debt on a dollar-for-dollar basis to prevent a sudden stop from escalating into a collapse. Pakistan’s debt-servicing obligation for this year amounts to $21.5 billion, while its reserves stand at $21.389 billion. This situation indicates that the country possesses just enough to meet its obligations for one year, assuming all creditors remain patient simultaneously. This scenario does not constitute a financial cushion but rather represents a precarious balance. Also read: Mark Carney is showing the centre still has a place in an age of extremes Someone else’s playbook Pakistan is not unique in facing this risk. Turkey employed a similar strategy for years, wherein the central bank utilised currency swaps, initially with domestic banks and subsequently with Qatar’s central bank and China’s PBOC, to artificially inflate headline reserves while the underlying critical figures deteriorated. In May 2023, after excluding these swaps, Turkey’s net reserves became negative, amounting to minus $151 million, marking the first occurrence of such a situation since 2002. Consequently, the lira depreciated by 44 percent within that year alone. Sri Lanka exemplifies the potential outcome of this trajectory without corrective measures. By May 2022, the finance ministry acknowledged that the country had approximately $25 million in usable reserves, rather than billions, while facing billions in maturing debt. Consequently, fuel ships remained anchored off Colombo because the country lacked dollars to unload them. The country subsequently defaulted on $51 billion in external debt weeks later. In Pakistan’s favour, substantive developments have emerged. The current account deficit significantly narrowed in July and August of this fiscal year. Remittances reached $3.66 billion in August, representing a substantial and increasing inflow of funds that require no repayment. Import cover also exceeded three months for the first time since 2020. These figures do not reflect a stagnant nation; rather, they indicate a country that has begun to finance its expenditures more independently and rely less on external assistance. Regrettably, the narrative in Islamabad does not reflect this reality, as it is less immediate and appealing than the portrayal of the Prime Minister expressing gratitude for a situation largely sustained by external patience. A rented mansion appears identical to an owned one until the landlord demands its return. Pakistan has begun establishing its own foundation and should avoid presenting temporary measures as permanent solutions. Bidisha Bhattacharya is ThePrint Consulting Editor (Economics) and an Associate Fellow, Chintan Research Foundation. She tweets @Bidishabh. Views are personal. (Edited by Prashant Dixit)

Consequently, fuel ships remained anchored off Colombo because the country lacked dollars to unload them. The country subsequently defaulted on $51 billion in external debt weeks later.

In Pakistan’s favour, substantive developments have emerged. The current account deficit significantly narrowed in July and August of this fiscal year. Remittances reached $3.66 billion in August, representing a substantial and increasing inflow of funds that require no repayment. Import cover also exceeded three months for the first time since 2020. These figures do not reflect a stagnant nation; rather, they indicate a country that has begun to finance its expenditures more independently and rely less on external assistance. Regrettably, the narrative in Islamabad does not reflect this reality, as it is less immediate and appealing than the portrayal of the Prime Minister expressing gratitude for a situation largely sustained by external patience. A rented mansion appears identical to an owned one until the landlord demands its return. Pakistan has begun establishing its own foundation and should avoid presenting temporary measures as permanent solutions. Bidisha Bhattacharya is ThePrint Consulting Editor (Economics) and an Associate Fellow, Chintan Research Foundation. She tweets @Bidishabh. Views are personal. (Edited by Prashant Dixit)
