editorials.title: ‘Srishti’s crime is empathy’: Who is the young artist jailed for supporting Noida workers’ protest?
editorials.passage:
“There is my friend, my sister,” said Pinky Kumari, her face lighting up with a smile. She was pointing to a photograph on display at an art exhibition in Shahbad Dairy, a low-income neighbourhood in North Delhi, on September 6.

The photograph showed Srishti Gupta, a 28-year-old artist, addressing a group of women, who were listening attentively. Gupta used to run basic literacy classes for the women of Shahbad Dairy, Kumari recalled.

A few steps away from this exhibit, scraps carrying children’s messages for Gupta adorned a sheet of sky-blue chart paper that hung from a string. “Miss you Srishti didi,” many of the messages read, using the Hindi word for elder sister as a mark of respect. Some of the children told Scroll that Gupta besides teaching them art also helped them revise their school lessons.

The residents of the neighbourhood have not met with Gupta since April 11, when she was detained by Uttar Pradesh Police for allegedly inciting violence during a workers’ protest in Noida, an industrial city in the National Capital Region. Her friends, who describe her as an “illegally imprisoned artist”, had organised the exhibition in Shahbad Dairy to raise awareness about her incarceration.

In April, thousands of industrial workers hit the streets in Noida to demand an increase in their wages, which had not been revised for many of them since 2014. In solidarity with them, Gupta had joined the protests alongside fellow activists associated with the Left-leaning Progressive Artists’ League. She was among the first few protesters to be arrested and has now spent more than five months in prison.

On September 1, the Allahabad High Court came down heavily on the authorities investigating cases related to the protests. The court pulled up the district magistrate of Gautam Buddha Nagar, of which Noida is a part, and the Uttar Pradesh Police for “concocting” stories about Akriti Chaudhary, another young artist who was picked up with Gupta.

However, Gupta and the other activists remain behind bars because the Uttar Pradesh Police has filed several cases against them in connection with the workers’ protest. Gupta has as many as 11 against her. She has yet to secure bail in two of them.

Gupta was born and raised in Amethi, a small town in Uttar Pradesh’s Awadh region. In 2016, the year she finished school, she moved to Delhi to study fine art at Delhi University’s College of Art.

Her course was primarily focused on printmaking and offered few opportunities to explore spaces beyond the college campus, said Vinod Karki, her batchmate and a fellow member of the Progressive Artists’ League. He described the process of creating art by printing as a physically intense and engaging process which requires artists to stay with their machines for long durations of time.

“Often, we did not even find the time to eat properly,” Karki explained. “Srishti would insist that all of us have lunch together. If somebody was unable to join, she brought them food and made sure they ate.”

In their four years at college, he was repeatedly struck by how much Gupta cared about other people. She was not very interested in politics at the time, Karki recalled. That, however, changed after she went to Visva-Bharati, the university founded by Rabindranath Tagore in 1921, for a master’s degree in fine arts.

Gupta reached Kala Bhavana, the university’s fine arts department, in 2020 and spent about four years in the world that Tagore had built in Bengal’s Santiniketan. Karki, who stayed in touch with her during those years, said that their phone conversations at the time reflected her newfound Leftist outlook.

“She talked a lot about Palestine,” he remembered. “How does capitalism work? Why are politicians the way they are? These were the questions that we discussed at length.”

As Gupta’s worldview expanded in Santiniketan, so did her relationship with art. Alongside her studies, she wrote poetry and picked up local handicrafts.

The exhibition in Shahbad Dairy, too, was strewn with objects from Santiniketan. There were reams of handmade paper as well as rope, both of which Gupta learned how to make from the Santhals, an Adivasi community, who live in and around Santiniketan.

Visva-Bharati alumnus Maksud Ali Mondal, 33, met Gupta during her time at the university. He had already graduated by then and was working out of a studio in Boner Pukur Danga, a Santhal village near Santiniketan.

Gupta used to visit the village frequently and formed a lasting relationship with its Adivasi residents. Mondal made it a point to tell Scroll that her relationship with the community was not an extractive one.

“She did not romanticise their landscape,” he said over the phone from Amsterdam. “Her approach was very sensitive. To this day, I get calls from those villagers asking me if Srishti is doing alright and when she will be released from prison.”

Gupta was so invested in the village that upon completing her master’s in 2022, she decided to follow in Mondal’s footsteps and stay there for a couple of years more. He even saw her learn how to sow paddy from the farmers in the village. That was her way of becoming one with the community, he contended. “She saw art as a way of connecting with people,” he added.

Mondal was, therefore, not surprised by Gupta’s turn to activism after she returned to Delhi in 2023. He saw her presence at the workers’ protest in Noida as not very different from her efforts to learn paddy farming from the Santhals of Boner Pukur Danga.

In Delhi, Gupta was drawn to an alternative strand of Left politics that is not restricted to contesting elections but focuses on grassroots activism in the working-class settlements that dot the city’s industrial suburbs.

An initiative that resonated deeply with Gupta was running community libraries for women and children in neighbourhoods such as Karawal Nagar and Shahbad Dairy. That is how she began volunteering in Shahbad Dairy and eventually moved there.

Besides community work, Gupta regularly went to protests in and around the city, such as the pickets her fellow activists organised outside brand outlets that they saw as complicit in the genocide in Gaza. Her participation in the Noida workers’ protest, her friends say, must be seen in this context.

But Uttar Pradesh Police’s chargesheets in the cases against Gupta paint a different picture. “Her main responsibility was to make posters and paintings for protests and incite workers,” reads one of these chargesheets, which describes her as a “key conspirator”.

The police have linked Gupta to a host of Leftist organisations such as the Revolutionary Workers’ Party of India, Mazdoor Bigul and Naujawan Bharat Sabha. They have also concluded that her “ideology” is “Maoism” because she possessed “books related to revolution”. One of these books is supposedly linked to the Communist Party of India (Maoist), a banned, far-Left organisation.

However, the police investigation against Gupta has itself become a subject of controversy. Her fellow activists have put out videos on social media which suggest that the police tried to plant evidence in her house after she had been arrested. The police have denied this accusation and claim that they went to her house in compliance with a court order.

“Her [Srishti’s] crime is empathy,” said Shuddhabrata Sengupta, a Delhi-based artist who has known Gupta for years and visited her in jail recently. “She was concerned about the lives of working-class people and their children. That is what has been criminalised.”

Mondal, the artist who first met Gupta in Santiniketan, concurred. Politics for her, he asserted, was not about political parties and their agendas, but primarily about being an ethical artist. As someone who came from a small-town, middle-class family that had nothing to do with art, she wanted to make a living as an artist without compromising on her beliefs.

“She used to ask me how I survive without a job because she had never seen someone do that while making art,” Mondal recalled. “I would tell her about funding and grants. She had questions about taking money from capitalists who fund ecological artists and, at the same time, deforest acres and acres of land.”

Before Gupta was arrested, her family did not know that such questions shaped her practice as an artist or about her engagement with Left activism. One of her relatives, who spoke to Scroll on the condition of anonymity fearing retribution from the police, said that they only supported her in pursuing art professionally because they appreciated her talent.

Gupta’s teachers from Visva-Bharati, too, declined interview requests citing university rules about talking to the press. Delhi’s artist community has also not spoken up in her support, as Sengupta, the artist quoted earlier in this piece, has repeatedly pointed out.

For friends and fellow activists, though, Gupta was more than an artist. “She did not confine herself to art,” stated Karki, her batchmate from college, adding that she was deeply involved in the day-to-day life of the communities she worked with.

In the initial months after returning to Delhi, Gupta used to spend most of her time in the Progressive Artists’ League studio located in the south-eastern part of the city. But once she immersed herself in the community library project in Shahbad Dairy, she decided to move into a room there.

“Before I met her, I used to think that art meant drawing,” said Naureen Sabba, a 26-year-old student-activist who Gupta lived with in Shahbad Dairy for eight months. “She broke my notions about artists. She told me about artists who stayed with marginalised people and voiced their concerns through their art.”

Gupta touched the lives of the neighbourhood’s other residents as well. In addition to teaching women and children, she helped with clearing garbage and organising health camps. Gupta’s friend, Pinky Kumari, remembered how she had accompanied her to the hospital after her son’s foot got burnt in an accident.

“She even found us a blood donor,” Kumari recollected. “I miss her a lot.”

editorials.title: A new book examines how socially entrenched food biases in India can endanger health
editorials.passage:
The fact that entrenched vegetarianism distances itself not just from meat, but also the meat-eater in physical as well as social ways, is largely ignored. That these social ways translate into the shameful practices of discrimination, denial, neglect, negligence, humiliation and untouchability is never recognised and acknowledged in these “simple” discourses. Separate plates, separate counters, separate kitchens, separate sinks and, indeed, separate cutlery, are all proof that untouchability is alive and well among Indians. What starts as not wanting to sit beside a meat-eater then transforms into them not being allowed into classrooms, not being allowed into educational institutions, and not being allowed to access education itself. “Legitimised” exclusion from all public and private spaces is precisely how the caste system operates. Ultimately, the entitled belief that vegetarians are superior is enough to demand that meat-eaters be kept away from them and perpetuates and sustains casteism in all its virulent forms.

In reality, these stereotypical behaviours are neither simple nor innocent because they have far-reaching consequences. The myth of India’s vegetarianism adeptly subsumes and erases nutritious and diverse cultures and traditions. The caste, class and religious overtones and undercurrents of this erasure can no longer be brushed aside as “culture”. This vegetarianism is also a kind of psychological, social, physical and economic violence that manifests through manipulation, erasure, imposition, segregation, discrimination, misinformation, abuse of law, exaggerated fragility, gaslighting, silence, collusion, etc.

When Buchanan-Hamilton (1807) was deputed by the East India Company to report on food practices, among other things, he documented the great difference in diet between castes and the importance of food as an index of social respectability. Up until the 1830s in Bombay and the 1840s in Bengal and the North-Western Provinces, prisoners were allowed to feed themselves. They were given an allowance with which to buy food from traders who visited the prisons and the firewood to cook for themselves. In this way it was hoped to save money and avoid the contentious issue of caste. But in a bid to strengthen jail discipline and decrease costs, the introduction of a system of a common mess resulted in protests within the prisons, including riots and assaults on warders. Although force was used to overcome the most violent resistance, opposition (particularly from oppressor-caste prisoners) lingered on into the 1850s and left the government wary of trying to impose a common mess on unwilling prisoners. It was also recognised that “both the preparation and consumption of food is a ritual and social act in Indian society in which whom one eats with and whom one accepts food from are governed by caste status, thus preventing people from eating as equals, and ensuring that meals are not pleasant conversational gatherings.”

In India, what people wish to consume and what they have to consume depends on innumerable factors such as caste, religion, culture, cost, geography, etc. Overall, 29% of women and 17% of men are vegetarians. However, “self-identification” into the categories of vegetarian/non-vegetarian is not reliable because even meat-eating people may self-identify as “vegetarian” out of social pressure.

Belligerent promotion of vegetarianism makes nutritious foods more and more difficult to access. All ASFs other than dairy are at risk of being erased or minimised.

Food imposition can happen in several ways. For instance, most of the advertisements, including by international brands, seem to cater only to the vegetarian sensibility. Vegetarian mayonnaise, burgers, curries, soups, pastas, etc., normalise and reinforce the myth of the “vegetarian India”. The messaging for the meat-eaters is that their foods are not meant for public display and that they are outliers in a majority vegetarian country.

The government, in collusion with accommodating researchers, tends to erase not just traditional foods from the plates of communities, but also data related to nutritional indicators such as heights, weights, anaemia, etc. Current attempts to remove the estimation of anaemia from the NFHS-6, lowering cutoffs for haemoglobin and lowering heights on the pretext that Indians are “genetically smaller” is dangerous and everyone needs to understand the implications of this policy change.

Boyd Orr, who was the director of the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation, said that if the diets of the poorer communities have to be made comparable to those whose diets were adequate for full health, it would require increased consumption of “the more expensive foodstuffs, viz, milk, eggs, butter, fruit, vegetables and meat” and would raise important “economic and political problems”. Shatrugna has also warned that a quest for cheaper foods based purely on calories would see a predominance of cereals, pulses and sugar in Indian diets.

This is very much the crux of the problem of malnutrition in India – there is little political will to create level playing fields for all citizens. In spite of the National Food Security Act (2013) making food a constitutional right, there is a general belief among the elite and middle class that these are “freebies”. What is implied is that families and individuals are responsible for feeding themselves, and if they don’t, they themselves are to blame. The gaze, as with other social issues, is mostly not on policies, programs, structures and institutions, but on individuals and communities.

The burden of addressing animal welfare and climate change is placed on the shoulders of the poorest in the country who are already staggering under numerous other precarities. Through skilled data jugglery, data erasure and arbitrarily changing cutoffs, malnutrition in its many forms will soon cease to be a public health concern on paper. Sadly, there is nothing really “pure” about our plates. They are contaminated not just with adulterants like toxins and heavy metals, but also by caste, religion, gender, politics, ideology and propaganda.

Excerpted with permission from The Meat of the Matter: How the Politics of Food Shapes Our Health, Sylvia Karpagam, HarperCollins India.

editorials.title: If Trump slaps tariffs, India should be ready to push back
editorials.passage:
The United States and India have had issues before. A whole bunch of them. The strategic partnership has taken almost two and a half decades of dedicated work from both sides to overcome the hesitations of history. One feels, however, that ties have now reached an inflection point. The next 30 days — the leeway Trump has in deciding to slap tariffs or opt for a waiver — might dictate the course for the next 30 years, or more.

What I found indicative is the changing mood in New Delhi. When it became clear that the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act would become a reality with Donald Trump’s signature, the MEA issued a statement that may reasonably be called “stern” by India’s tepid standards. Several things were made clear at once: New Delhi has been telling Washington behind the scenes that passing such legislation leading to the imposition of tariffs will have grave consequences for bilateral ties and global energy markets, and that this time India is in no mood to be accommodative.

Going by the way India has historically treated American tantrums — which is to bend the knee and cope silently while claiming to be ‘strategically autonomous’ — this was quite extraordinary. It suggested that patience in New Delhi is finally running thin, and issues that earlier would never be leaked into the public domain may increasingly become part of a concerted, even official pushback.
South Block has a habit of issuing ultra-sanitised statements and generous word salads of nothingness, so if Washington has even a rudimentary understanding of India’s strategic culture, it should take note.

You won’t find Prime Minister Narendra Modi publicly rebuking Trump or sharing an AI-generated meme on social media, of course. But indications abound of India’s latent indignation, frustration and even anger at repeatedly finding itself at the receiving end of Trump’s hare-brained policies, abuses, trade wars and military misadventures. If the MEA’s unusually strong reaction is one indication of it, unnamed “highly placed” officials unburdening themselves in the media is another. A very Indian trait.

On Monday, one such Indian official was quoted in The Economic Times as saying that “the US is not taking the right approach. Double standards are being applied and may not achieve the desired result at a time when oil supplies from Saudi Arabia are also under stress… The US needs to work with India and not against it.”
This is the Indian state publicly telling those who matter in the US that it can’t be business as usual. Of course, the legislation also includes China, the largest buyer of Russian energy, as well as Turkey and Hungary within its ambit, but no one in New Delhi is under any illusion.

As Kirti Vardhan Singh, minister of state for external affairs, said on record: “We will take decisive steps to ensure the strength and stability of our nation and its population. We maintain an independent foreign policy; we do not align ourselves based on the dictates of other nations but rather act in the best interests of our own country.”

The bit of rhetoric aside, the thrust is clear. If Trump moves ahead with another set of tariffs or tightens pressure on India to stop buying Russian oil, the strategic partnership will undergo a structural and psychological rupture from which it may never fully recover.

There are multiple reasons behind this tiredness and indignation. Part of it is due to the utter shamelessness of Washington, DC. Secondary sanctions are consistently framed by the US as weapons of morality — there is an element of sanctimony attached to these economic and financial tools designed to punish bad actors, deter aggression and uphold the global order. Yet, this law, which seeks to squeeze Russia’s revenue and force Vladimir Putin’s hand in ending the war, has a neat little exemption embedded for America’s own imports of low-enriched uranium (LEU) from Russia.

America’s domestic nuclear power industry relies heavily on Russian LEU to keep its reactors running. Hawkish lawmakers across both sides of the aisle who profess unrelenting hostility towards a “murderous Putin” conveniently find Russian LEU bereft of all evil.

Or take Trump’s proclamation that he is working on a “massive” deal to buy potash from Belarus, ruled by Putin’s ally Lukashenko. It has also been reported by The New York Times that the Trump White House is considering signing business deals with Russia and aiming for a “reset” in ties while Trump goes about targeting India for buying Russian oil.

Double standards such as these strip the legislation of any semblance of moral justification and transform the issue into a fundamental question of sovereignty and self-respect.

India also feels singled out. While its purchase of Russian seaborne crude, essential for the energy security of 1.4 billion people, is frequently under scrutiny, China gets a free pass despite being the biggest purchaser of Russian energy by far. The reason is simple. China possesses leverage against the US and can impose serious costs; India does not.

This legislation is being passed at a time when Xi Jinping is due to arrive in Washington on a state visit, and Trump is laying out the proverbial red carpet — from greeting the Chinese president on the tarmac (a rare gesture for an American president) to a military flyover. The arrival ceremony, according to a White House readout, “will feature 479 military personnel, representing all branches of the United States Armed Forces.”

Meanwhile, The New York Times reports that the US and China are deep into negotiations over a ‘comprehensive trade truce’. The report says that while the US is non-committal beyond keeping the truce for six months, China is pushing for an extension for as long as possible. And if Washington dithers, China will simply choke off the supply of rare earths and magnets. A Financial Times report says Beijing is doing just that.

Translated, it means that Trump is in no position to impose any further tariffs on China, even though Beijing’s strategic, military and economic lifeline to Moscow is far more comprehensive and consequential than New Delhi’s strictly transactional energy purchases.

Yet, since Trump is wary of Beijing’s capacity for asymmetric retaliation and its political will to inflict severe, targeted pain on the American economy, he will opt for the soft target instead. India is being lined up to be made an example of.
For years, India has bent over backwards to accommodate American whims and sanctions, often at significant cost to its national interests. We have repeatedly tied our energy procurement policy to the volatility of American foreign policy. When Washington demanded that we zero out our crude imports from Iran — a traditional, reliable, proximate supplier — New Delhi readily complied.
We similarly backed away from Venezuelan crude under US pressure until Trump implemented a regime change in the country and declared Venezuelan oil to be kosher. Our imports swung back to nearly 5 per cent in July 2026 from zero in 2022-23.

We absorbed the economic friction, paid a premium for alternative supplies and alienated regional partners in the process. We did this to prioritise the “strategic partnership” with the US. But what has this historical accommodation yielded? It has reinforced an assumption in Washington that India can be pressured, squeezed and ultimately brought to heel without any meaningful pushback.

This time, however, the structural realities of the global economy make capitulation impossible. The defiance we are currently seeing from New Delhi is not born of a desire to antagonise Washington; India’s back is against the wall, and we simply cannot afford to stop procuring Russian oil.

The global energy market is under immense strain, not least because traditional West Asian supply lines are severely choked. Oil traffic has slowed to a trickle in the Strait of Hormuz while the Houthis have laid siege to Bab el-Mandeb. These bottlenecks are a direct consequence of the Trump administration’s misadventures, scatterbrained policy shifts and the ill-advised war against Iran that has destabilised the region and affected the two most important energy corridors in West Asia.
For India, which imports 90 per cent of its energy, a $10 increase in the price of crude expands India’s annual bill by nearly $14 billion. It will send shockwaves through the economy, drive up inflation, widen the current account deficit and deplete foreign exchange reserves.

With West Asian oil flows severely disrupted and crude from the region several dollars dearer than Russian Urals, India procured more than 50 per cent of its energy needs in July from Moscow. Russia’s supplies have been steady, predictable and cost-efficient. If America forces India to reject this source and makes us pay for its foreign policy clusterfucks, New Delhi should be prepared to treat the US as an adversary and take proportionate countermeasures.

We should not shy away from reciprocal tariffs on American agricultural products such as almonds and apples, slap curbs on Big Tech and reduce energy imports. The confrontation is not a step to be taken lightly, since America remains India’s biggest export market, and the government must communicate the imperatives behind the decision clearly and in a timely manner to the public.

The MSME might be badly affected, and the government will need to alleviate their pain through specific policies. Markets may react poorly in the short term, export-reliant sectors may face headwinds, and the diplomatic friction will be intense.

This reckoning cannot be kicked any further down the road. Yielding to the Trump administration’s unilateral and unpredictable demands may invite even more coercion in the future.

Conversely, absorbing this adversarial pressure could serve as a catalyst for our growth. Being forced to navigate an increasingly weaponised American financial and trade system may accelerate our efforts towards genuine economic diversification, compel us to speed up non-dollar-denominated trade mechanisms and independent payment gateways. The pathway was recently set out at the Brics Summit.

Severe American pressure might also necessitate the exploration of a pragmatic, clear-eyed modus vivendi with China. If both New Delhi and Beijing find themselves navigating American financial coercion, the shared difficulty might open unexpected avenues. While our border disputes and strategic competition with China remain deeply entrenched, economic pragmatism could force a localised de-escalation.

For instance, the thaw in ties has already resulted in a significant jump in Indian exports to China, which rose 39 per cent to $9.6 billion during April-August 2026-27. Trade with core Brics members — China, South Africa, Brazil and Russia — accounted for 9.2 per cent of India’s total exports in April-August 2026-27, up from 8.1 per cent a year earlier, according to commerce ministry data.

Ultimately, not capitulating to American shenanigans will make India more self-reliant and a far more self-confident power. It will prove to the world, and more importantly to ourselves, that our rise is not contingent on the goodwill of a distant superpower. The partnership with the US has been valuable, but if the price of that partnership is the surrender of our autonomy and the sabotage of our economic and energy security, it is a price we cannot pay.

(Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Greenland, Trump and the power of no
editorials.passage:
On Tuesday evening, the United States, Denmark and Greenland will sign an agreement on the contentious issue of the US presence and operations in Greenland. The text of the agreement will spell out its details, but from the comments by President Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, it is clear that all three have made compromises. This is despite Frederiksen’s claim that Danish sovereignty will not be compromised and Greenland’s leader emphasising that the agreement will serve his territory’s interests. Greenland is an autonomous part of Denmark.

It is Trump’s climbdown that is most significant. This is because the agreement will no doubt be far removed from his original demand: that Denmark should sell Greenland to the US. He had told the US Congress in his State of the Union address in 2025 that the US would get it one way or another. The implication of these words was that he wanted to make Greenland an integral part of the US. The unmistakable parallel was with Alaska, which the US bought from Russia in 1867 and which is now a US state.

Trump’s post on Truth Social on September 19 does not mention either the territory’s purchase or Greenland’s merger with the US. Rather, it focuses on unimpeded US access to Greenland. It further notes that both Denmark and Greenland have agreed that “from now on, no U.S. adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval."

He has further stated that the agreement will be of indefinite duration. In the post, Trump has also asserted, “We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many. We will work with the people of Greenland in its development and construction”.

Further making the point that the agreement is a “great one” for all three parties and their allies, the post concludes with these rhapsodic words: “This is a dream come true for the United States of America, one that is very important, historic, and special”. Special it may be, but it is not even remotely what he wanted in the first place.

This deal represents the vintage Trumpian negotiating style drawn from his days in real estate. He begins by making extravagant and outrageous demands that completely ignore the norms of interstate conduct or even the principles of the world order which, ironically, the US itself established after the Second World War. When these are resisted, as they were by the Danes on this occasion, he puts enormous pressure even on his allies. This can extend to threatening the use of force.

At one stage, some European countries were compelled to demonstrate through symbolic actions on the ground in Greenland that Trump’s use of force would be met with resistance. He increases pressure through more threats. In this case, it was through increasing his abuse of the NATO alliance. However, while all this is going on in public, he is also willing to negotiate a deal and goes about it quietly.

In his Truth Social post, he stated: “At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America."

Once this agreement is signed, it will be studied closely. Equally meticulously, the process leading to its acceptance by the three countries will also be scrutinised. The first to go through the fine print of the agreement will be the Danish opposition. Mette Frederiksen formed the government for the third time this June, but she is politically vulnerable.

Both the Danish opposition and the opposition parties in Greenland would seek particularly to determine whether this agreement, by allowing unimpeded access to the US, as Trump is claiming, will, in reality, dilute Danish sovereignty to a nullity. Besides, Greenland has aspirations to become independent and sovereign itself.

Trump has indicated that the US will have access to Greenland forever. Can an agreement signed by an autonomous territory remain binding if that territory becomes sovereign? That can only be the case if an independent Greenland considers itself the successor state to Denmark. Thus, this may work in international law, but will it be politically acceptable in Greenland?

There is no doubt that the NATO countries would have been anxious for the Danes and the US to come to an agreement. This is for two principal reasons. The first is that NATO and Europe cannot do without the security provided by the US. Yes, there are serious endeavours being made among European countries to take charge of their own security and not be dependent on the US. However, that, if at all feasible, lies in the future.

Today, the Europeans are still struggling to come to terms with the blow to the continent’s security from the continuing war in Ukraine. With an uncompromising Russia, it is essential for Europe to retain US support even if Trump, despite the new sanctions that may be imposed on Russia and states that do business with it, does not have his predecessor’s passion against it.

The US, Canada and Europe have common interests in ensuring that the Arctic region, which is undergoing profound changes on account of climate change, remains within their sphere of influence. There are prospects of Arctic shipping routes being opened in the years to come. That would greatly interest the Chinese.

This is apart from the natural resources that may lie under Greenland’s huge territory, which is permanently covered by ice that may melt in the future. This too would have been an important element in the strategic thinking in Copenhagen, European capitals and Nuuk.

These factors will lead to great introspection in Denmark and Greenland even if the new US-Denmark-Greenland agreement goes far beyond the 1951 US-Denmark agreement which had provided for US-Danish consultations before the US took action to expand its presence in Greenland. It also allowed Danish officers to be present at US bases, though in small numbers. However, it was obvious that despite these provisions, the US made deployments in Greenland in accordance with its security requirements. Thus, during the Cold War, the US had, at one stage, over 10,000 troops and 17 bases in Greenland.

After the Cold War was over, it brought down that number to just one base and troop levels to the low hundreds. All in all, European countries will lean on the Danish and Greenlandic opposition to go along with the agreement.

Finally, Denmark and Greenland's success, supported by European countries, in not allowing the US to blatantly ‘buy’ Greenland, together with Trump’s climbdown, will send a lesson to all countries, especially those like Iran, which are battling him, that there is substance in the sentiment behind TACO — Trump Always Chickens Out. That may be an exaggeration, but it is good to stand up to Trump’s threats and theatrics because that is the way to deal with him, rather than simply caving in to the first pressure he puts on a country.

(The writer is a former Indian diplomat who served as India’s Ambassador to Afghanistan and Myanmar, and as secretary, the Ministry of External Affairs. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Charles vs Charles: Why Earl Spencer’s Diana bombshell is not a dud
editorials.passage:
One thing that many people do not understand is that royals, titled aristocrats and feudals — and even celebrities and politicians — live in parallel universes. One is their public universe comprising their careers and interactions with the wider (and impersonal) society. The other is their private lives, comprising immediate family and very close personal friends, with whom the dynamics are very different. And it is impossible to really gauge those private relationships from the outside.

In the shadow-boxing match currently playing out in media and social media between the two Charles’ — Windsor and Spencer — over Diana, this factor is exceedingly important. All those who have been commenting for or against both are outsiders; none are from even the extended royal family and none are personal friends of either party. So none could possibly know what the relationship between them was like during the Wales’ tumultuous, unhappy marriage.

Rage was evident in Charles Spencer’s now-famous eulogy at Diana’s funeral in 1997. The conversation recounted in his book Swan Song: Diana, My Sister that is now the centre of controversy could well have been the trigger. For all that he and Diana were estranged when she died, blood does run thicker than water. And any offhand remark about Diana from his ex-brother-in-law — typical actually among the elite where feelings are underplayed — could have set him off.

Earl Spencer avers that the then Prince of Wales (and now King Charles III) ended a fraught one-sided phone call with the hissed words, “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.” A shocked Charles Spencer ends the call with “I can’t believe you just said that!” Many have insisted that the “ex-husband Charles” simply could not have said that as he was grieving, also implying that “brother Charles” was merely aggrieved, then and now. Hard for anyone to say, as outsiders.

Seeing King Charles III now, smiling, snow-haired, wrinkled and undergoing prolonged cancer treatment with stoic fortitude, it may be hard to believe he would say anything so spiteful. But Charles then isn’t the same as Charles now. Back then he knew he had been outplayed by Diana in the public arena, his one true love was reviled and he was doomed to play second fiddle to his mother for the foreseeable future. Would that have made him a very genial person?

Most photos featuring the then Prince Charles in the company of Princess Diana, in hindsight, show a distinct lack of chemistry and widening emotional distance. Diana’s eyes were initially frank and adoring; later those same dark blue eyes looked hurt, wistful and guarded. His expressions were mostly annoyed or sullen mostly; broadly speaking, he looked unhappy. It is hard to keep up a façade when living in a fishbowl, with cameras trained to catch every grimace and pout.

Charles III, for all his positive image now, was known to be petulant and peevish about his lot in life as the heir apparent: not able to do anything he really wanted, from reviving classical architecture to marrying a divorcee. While decorum demanded that he show grief at his ex-wife’s tragic demise, his human side may have realised how this altered his hitherto gloomy personal future. So, a private phone call with Diana’s estranged brother may well have elicited rare candour.

It would have been impossible for Earl Spencer to reveal hurt or anger at that purported remark just then, especially with the Queen making rare concessions when it came to Diana’s funeral. Instead, he chose to deliver a defiant eulogy, a shot across the royal bows if there ever was one. Such rage could not have been triggered only by the paparazzi pressure that led to Diana’s last catastrophic car-ride.

There had to be more private causes for Spencer’s impassioned speech.
Buckingham Palace’s official line, as evident from its response to Spencer’s version of the aftermath of Diana’s death, is that he hallucinating, if not outright fibbing: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.” People, including the Earl, have called this gaslighting.

There is a kernel of truth in that, of course. But just as “fraternal grief” could cloud reason” and “affect judgment”, so could spousal grief, surely? If Diana’s ex-husband was indeed grief-stricken by her tragic death as his friends and proxies insist, could his recollection of any exchanges with others in those first few hours and days be hazy too? That may be why there was no outright denial, only protestations by others that he could never have made such a remark.

Outsiders, including sundry former palace officials, claim Charles insisted staff should never criticise Diana. But that does not indicate that he necessarily felt obliged to follow his own advice. He simply re-emphasised the line that separated him (including all the Royals, current and former) from the hoi polloi; it was a lese majeste warning rather than a call to join him in respecting her memory. How did the question of staff criticising Diana arise in the first place, anyway?

By rekindling the memories of those sad days in September 1997, Earl Spencer has focused attention on how Charles and Camilla finally began an image makeover after Diana’s death, culminating in their current narrative of a devoted old couple, rather than the pair that made the People’s Princess so unhappy. Had Diana still been around, the path would have been much rockier, if not impossible. The book would also remind Charles about the man he was then, if not now.

Only the two Charles know what transpired, and no one on the outside is in a position to determine whether such a conversation could ever happen, whether both Charles’ were grief-stricken or only one, and why not. One Charles felt the need to lance the boil and let out the pus rather than put yet another band-aid to obscure it. For the other Charles it is a chance to see if Diana’s ghost has finally been laid to rest and he and Camilla have now secured the public’s affection.

(The author is a freelance writer. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely that of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Mecca Defence Pact: A Month on, Where the Saudi-Turkey-Pak Alliance Falls Short
editorials.passage: Last month, the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement was signed between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan with a far-reaching clause akin to Article 5 of the NATO Agreement. It establishes a trilateral collective-defence framework whose operative sentence reads: “An armed attack on one signatory shall be regarded as an attack against them all.” The agreement, signed on 7 August, was already being touted as “Islamic NATO”. However, in less than a month, seeds of doubt have begun to sprout.Collective-defence pacts are meant to deter wars. Yet, if signatories make sweeping promises without the military integration, decision-making mechanisms, and escalation controls needed to carry them out, the limits of these promises come under question. In the absence of these clearly established mechanisms, the agreement is facing serious difficulties in responding to an escalating confrontation. Its strategic significance, therefore, depends less on the declaration of mutual commitment than on whether its members can translate political solidarity into credible and coordinated capabilities for deterrence and escalation management.Why India Must Read the Mecca Pact Beyond the 'Islamic NATO' TagEach signatory has different strategic motivations. Saudi Arabia seeks greater regional leverage and enhanced deterrence to protect its economic transformation and critical national infrastructure. Turkey seeks a cooperative framework to manage regional spillover, counter unfavourable strategic shifts, and align its industrial and military capabilities with those of its partners. Pakistan, the only nuclear power among the three, aims to leverage its nuclear and conventional military capabilities while deepening economic and defence ties with major West Asian countries.But the central challenge for them lies in converting political solidarity into a sufficiently credible and flexible deterrence without creating commitments that outpace their capacity to act.  The important question, therefore, is whether the ambiguity surrounding how these capabilities might be employed together is sufficient to make potential adversaries, including Iran, Israel, or the Houthis, less willing to test the resolve of any one member.Although all three countries have emphasised political solidarity in response to growing uncertainty across the region, the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement remains largely a political commitment and lacks some of the military mechanisms necessary for sustained coordination.  The pact is laden with symbolic significance as the three possess military capabilities which are not complementary. Saudi Arabia contributes substantial financial muscle and advanced Western-origin air and missile defence systems. Turkey offers a military industrial base that manufactures advanced drones and missile systems and is a part of NATO, but is increasingly shifting towards indigenous technologies. Pakistan contributes a large military force, primarily operating Chinese equipment, with significant combat experience and a nuclear arsenal.The fact is that defence-industrial cooperation does not automatically produce military interoperability. Building interoperability across these disparate architectures will require years of investment in common communication standards, data links, doctrines, and training. If effectively integrated, these capabilities could pose the threat of collective retaliation. But this interoperability and integration remain the pact’s most difficult and consequential challenge.The threat perceptions and strategic priorities are divergent. Riyadh remains primarily concerned with Gulf security and the protection of critical infrastructure from the Houthis, while Ankara’s concerns extend across Syria, Iraq, the Eastern Mediterranean, including Cyprus, Greece and the Caucasus. Islamabad remains heavily focused on India.These divergent priorities raise questions among potential adversaries about whether all three members would incur the costs and risks necessary to defend one another.No wonder External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, when asked about India’s reaction to the agreement said: “There are live military situations which each of the signatories face, what has the Mecca pact done in response to that?”In the aftermath of the agreement, regional actors continued to challenge the security arrangement. The Houthis attacked Saudi strategic targets, including crude oil tank farms in Jazan and Abha on 8 September, as well as facilities belonging to state oil giant Aramco. Israel struck Abu Duhur Air Base, near the Turkish border, shortly after Turkish security officials had visited the area as part of Ankara’s effort to support the development of Syria’s post-civil-war military capabilities. None of these attacks triggered the mutual security promises of the agreement.The Houthis’ lightning advance along Yemen's Red Sea coast, which included Perim Island in the Strait of Bab al-Mandab and Mocha, apparently with direct guidance from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, opened a new front in Iran's war with the US, while also bringing the Houthis into direct confrontation with Saudi Arabia.On 2 September, Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s Security Chief, wrote on X, “You will soon witness that Iran’s new strategy across the battlefield, diplomacy, and countering the economic siege will shatter your foundations.”On 10 September, Pakistan Foreign Ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said there had been no discussions about a military reaction under the Mecca Agreement in response to ‌the Houthis’ attacks on Saudi Arabia. He said, “When time comes, (we) will act under the agreement.” Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said that the three countries “did not need to respond to aggression with aggression”. The Mecca agreement is an umbrella agreement, “purely for defensive purposes”, and aimed primarily at strengthening regional peace and stability.The absence of a coordinated military response from the three partners beyond conventional diplomatic condemnations illustrates the gap between political statements, and military action. Unless the pact develops mechanisms for joint planning, intelligence sharing, military exercises, and coordinated responses to aggression, its declaratory commitment may remain insufficient to establish credible collective deterrence.  Each of these countries has regional issues, be it with Yemen, Greece, and Cyprus or India. In a case of conflict, members would be forced to choose between the alliance’s credibility and their own economic and geopolitical interests. There is thus a wide gap between political ambition and military response. 'Attack On One, Attack On All': Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Turkey Sign Defence PactWhen you analyse the Mecca Pact, one question that crops up is: who will provide security to whom? How will the arrangement work?The three countries in question are not neighbouring states. They have no land borders with one another. Then how exactly are the security guarantees expected to be delivered? None of them can boast of superpower status with unlimited military hardware.To evaluate how capacities and capabilities affect the Mecca agreement in general, and India in particular, we must look at how the alliance is structured. A simple answer to this can be derived from an analysis of the overall military capability of each of the nation states. The land forces are weighted towards Pakistan, with approximately 600,000 troops, followed by Turkey with 400,000 troops and Saudi Arabia with 200,000.In the air forces, the Turkish Air Force leads with a modernised, heavy-lift transport fleet. Its inventory includes 10 Airbus A400M Atlas strategic airlifters. Each A400M can carry 116 fully geared paratroopers or up to 37 tonnes of cargo. Turkey also has approximately 19 C-130s. A standard C-130 can carry 92 ground troops or 64 paratroopers. There are also 52 CN-235 aircraft, each of which can carry up to 44 troops. Therefore, there is an estimated single-wave troop lift of about a brigade-minus. They also have a mixed bag of 13-15 fighter aircraft squadrons.Saudi Arabia has an estimated 30-plus Lockheed C-130 Hercules and C-130J Super Hercules variants, as well as six Airbus A330 MRTT (Multi-Role Tanker Transport) aircraft. Each A330 can also be configured to fly up to 300 fully equipped troops, thereby giving it an estimated single-wave troop lift of less than a brigade. They have 15-17 squadrons of relatively modern American and European fighter aircraft.Pakistan has roughly 16 Lockheed C-130 Hercules variants, four Ilyushin Il-78 aerial tankers, and some CN-235 and Y-12 utility aircraft used for short-range movements. Its total estimated single-wave troop lift is less than two battalions. Its fighter squadrons total almost 25 squadrons, comprising mainly legacy fighters, but also including F-16s, JF-17s, and J-10CEs.The naval lift capabilities of Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan could dramatically expand the scope of the defence agreement. However, other than Turkey, the naval assets of the other two countries are comparatively nascent in size and designed for domestic security challenges. They are not classically designed for “out-of-area contingencies”.Turkey has the most sophisticated naval projection capability. The TCG Anadolu, a multi-purpose amphibious assault ship, acts as a floating command centre. It can carry a fully equipped battalion-sized marine task force of 940 troops, along with tanks and landing craft. It can deploy armed drones, like the Bayraktar TB3, giving it precision-strike capabilities during a naval deployment without needing land-based aircraft, but it is a drone carrier, not an aircraft carrier. Turkey fields several large tank landing ships (LSTs), each capable of carrying 350 troops and up to 20 MBTs (main battle tanks).Thus, the naval forces of each country are designed to meet specific regional security requirements. While inter-operability is possible, any such employment would create critical voids in the already limited naval assets. Theoretically speaking, if the alliance had to deploy a joint task force tomorrow, it would be safe to assume that Pakistan can provide raw manpower for dispatch to a regional staging ground, for which combined heavy lift capability would be required. Such a deployment would face interoperability challenges because it would entail a mix of Western (Airbus, Lockheed) and Eastern (Ilyushin) aircraft. The combined naval sealift assets could be used to sustain medium-scale military operations over limited periods. The next question is which country they expect to pose a common threat. Israel? Or Iran? A simultaneous offensive from both Turkey and Pakistan could pose a major threat to Iran. However, there have been no deliberate attacks on targets inside Turkey or Pakistan by Iran recently. In fact, Iran has reportedly been invited to join the trilateral agreement. Israel does not share land borders with all three. That leaves India.Let us break down this security matrix as probably perceived by Field Marshal Asim Munir. He hopes that in case of an Operation Sindoor-type conflict with India, Turkey would immediately reach out to assist Pakistan. So, Turkey would indirectly be at war with India. But Turkey is a part of NATO, and would India like to be at war with a NATO-backed country?The other partner is Saudi Arabia. If Pakistan is at war with India, then Saudi Arabia will support Pakistan, and therefore also be indirectly at war with India. The net security provider to Saudi Arabia is the USA. If Saudi Arabia is at war, then by virtue of their security agreement the US too would enter the war.  Now look at this from a hypothetical context. India, in response to any Pahalgam-like misadventure by Pakistan, would launch Operation Sindoor II. (India has already stated that Operation Sindoor is unfinished business.) Asim Munir will hope that such a response would draw Saudi Arabia and Turkey into the conflict, and if they do, then indirectly their net security providers would also be drawn into the conflict. Though this may sound absurd, and whether it will happen or not is conjecture, the possibility theoretically exists.Asim Munir is taking on a role in regional politics that he cannot sustain. Sooner or later, the veil will drop and his reality will be exposed. Turkey and Saudi Arabia are too involved in their own security issues to jump in aid of Pakistan. With the absence of land borders between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, their combined military capability and lack of compatibility, one can safely assume that the Mecca agreement is not an immediate threat to India. India must continue to analyse the collective ground, air, and naval capabilities of all three countries to arrive at logical and militarily sustainable conclusions. While doing so, there should be no let-up in modernising our military hardware. With the kind of mindset of our neighbour, we cannot afford to wish away the threat. Instead, we must prepare for the worst.Operation Sindoor and the Unfinished Business of Defence ReformsIndia has to reconstruct its stand on “strategic autonomy.” This is a time to make friends. The India-Saudi relationship, for example, has always been good. Prime Minister Narendra Modi recently visited Saudi Arabia in 2025. This bilateral relationship must be strengthened.  India-Turkey relations hit an all-time low given Turkey's open support to Pakistan over Kashmir and during Operation Sindoor last year. However, there is room for improvement, for which efforts must be made.Overall, the diplomatic effort towards the whole of West Asia needs recalibration. Sustained efforts with Iran will help nullify any adversity that the US-Israel-Iran war might have caused.Pakistan-Saudi Arabia defence cooperation is nothing new. They have had written agreements for decades. Pakistan has traditionally had a military presence in Saudi Arabia. Both Saudi Arabia and Turkey actively supported Pakistan during the 1971 Indo-Pak war, by providing fighter planes and other military wherewithal. There was no Mecca Agreement then. Therefore, India can surely expect similar support in any future Indo-Pak war. However, given their own regional security issues, anything substantial may not be practical in the present scenario.As deduced that unless the agreement’s political commitments are matched by credible capabilities and mechanisms for coordination, the Mecca agreement risks overpromising while underdelivering. Such a gap could not only weaken its deterrent value, but also complicate crisis management. No wonder the pact currently appears less like the foundation of a new deterrence architecture and more like a high-stakes political experiment. Its significance should therefore be assessed realistically rather than on the basis of promises it has not been designed to fulfil. It remains, like a rainbow in the sky, on a sunny day.(The authors are retired Major Generals of the Indian Army. This is an opinion piece, and the views expressed are the author’s own. The Quint neither endorses nor is responsible for them.)

editorials.title: Trump's Latest Media Ban Is a Dangerous Blow to Press Freedom
editorials.passage: Donald Trump’s fight with the media has escalated with the news that five major broadcast networks, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC, have suspended their pool coverage of the White House. Their decision comes after the Trump administration banned CNN, along with MS Now and Politico, from the White House for alleged “fake news” and “negative news” reporting. CNN was due to be the White House broadcast network responsible for covering the White House for the week beginning 21 September. In a joint statement the networks said: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting.”CNN, MS Now, and Politico have filed a lawsuit “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes”. According to the US constitution, the First Amendment states: “Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.”The once mighty White House Correspondents Association said on 19 September that the “action revoking access for journalists from CNN, Politico and MS Now violates the First Amendment […] The WHCA calls on the administration to immediately restore our colleagues’ access.”On the day after the ban was announced, CNN’s Betsy Klein, MS NOW’s Akayla Gardner and Politico’s Cheyenne Haslett all reported on having their badges taken away from them after showing up to work at the White House.Klein’s report on CNN argued reporting would continue and “we can do our job anywhere”. But while this is a commendable aim, it is a wrongheaded argument to make when you are also maintaining that you ought to be doing that job from inside the White House because access is an inalienable right.Martin Baron: A Free Press Is the First Line of Defence for DemocracyTrump likes to characterise his relationship with the press as open and transparent. And yet he has been embroiled in multiple court cases which have seen some media outlets, such as CBS, hoist the white flag, paying stupendous amounts of money for alleged unfair reporting or editing. The BBC is still facing a US$10 billion (£7.4 billion) lawsuit over a so-called “unfair edit” in a Panorama programme dating back to 2021.Meanwhile, the Associated Press (AP) is also involved in its own ongoing court action against the Trump government over its banning from Oval Office and Air Force One pool reporting. The ban was imposed following AP’s decision to continue using the internationally recognised geographical term the “Gulf of Mexico” – which Trump demanded be changed to the “Gulf of America”.Some media advocacy groups are condemning this latest blow to press freedom. Seth Stern from the Freedom of the Press Foundation said: “It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the People’s House for criticising the government. It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move.” Given that this White House, in particular the vice-president, J.D. Vance, is often heard parroting the cause of free speech, it is also deeply ironic.Many previous heads of government have clashed with the press in the past but stopped short of bans. Joe Biden restricted the number of press “hard passes” to the White House in 2023 from 1,417 to 975, but as Politico reported at the time, the administration argued this was “about ensuring those who hold them are actively working the beat”.Barack Obama’s Treasury Department was accused back in 2009 of intentionally trying to exclude a Fox News reporter from interviewing his administration’s “pay czar”, Kenneth Feinberg. This was put down to a miscommunication and was rectified by the administration. On 19 September, Obama told an audience at Colgate University which was discussing the newly introduced Trump press ban: “I’m trying to think what would have happened if I had said, you know what, Fox News, you’re outta here!” A Year On From His Second Inauguration, Trump 2.0 Has One Defining Word: PowerBut perhaps the former president whom Trump most resembles is Richard Nixon. One must not forget Nixon’s comments on the press, captured on his own secret audio tapes made from the White House in 1972. In a meeting with his national security advisors Henry Kissinger and Alexander Haig, he said: “Never forget the press is the enemy. The establishment is the enemy, the professors are the enemy.”Today, the organisations that have oversight of press access and coverage are toothless. There was a time when the WHCA was in charge of organising the press pool rotations and access to briefings and Air Force One. But now it has to bow before Trump’s decisions on granting access to media outlets that extol the virtues of his administration.According to Pew Research data (2022) only one in six media workers in the US are in a union. The country’s largest media union, the NewsGuild-CWA, with its 25,000 members, has still to comment.(Colleen Murrell is Full Professor in Journalism, Dublin City University. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article here.)
